stem: A DevOps team wants automated, continuous scanning of EC2 instances and container images in Amazon ECR for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs), without deploying agents to every instance manually. Which service natively provides this?

choices.text: AWS Config
Amazon Inspector, using agentless EC2 scanning via SSM and automatic ECR image scanning on push
AWS Trusted Advisor
CloudTrail Insights

explanation: Amazon Inspector automatically and continuously scans EC2 instances (via the SSM agent) and container images in ECR for software vulnerabilities and network reachability issues. Trusted Advisor provides best-practice checks but not CVE-level vulnerability scanning.

stem: A company running a fleet of on-premises VMware VMs needs to implement disaster recovery to AWS with sub-second replication and the ability to fail over entire servers within minutes, without re-architecting the application. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: AWS Backup
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
AWS DataSync
AWS Application Migration Service configured for one-time migration only

explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates on-premises or cloud servers at the block level to a low-cost staging area in AWS and can launch fully provisioned recovery instances within minutes during a failover, without requiring re-architecture. AWS Backup handles scheduled backups and restores, which typically has a longer RTO than continuous block-level replication.

stem: A company runs its primary application stack in us-east-1 and a fully provisioned standby stack in us-west-2. It wants automatic DNS failover to the standby Region if health checks against the primary fail, without manual DNS changes. What should be configured?

choices.text: A simple routing policy pointing only to the primary Region's endpoint
Route 53 failover routing policy with health checks on the primary endpoint, automatically routing to the secondary Region's endpoint on failure
Weighted routing split 50/50 between both Regions at all times
A CNAME record manually updated during an incident

explanation: Route 53 failover routing policy paired with health checks is designed for this active-passive DR pattern: it automatically shifts DNS resolution to the secondary record when the primary fails its health checks, with no manual intervention. Weighted routing would send some traffic to standby continuously, which isn't the described requirement, and manual CNAME updates defeat the automatic requirement.

stem: A company wants its Amazon Aurora MySQL database's data to be available for near-real-time recovery in a secondary Region with an RPO of a few seconds, and the ability to promote the secondary to a full read/write cluster during a regional disaster. Which Aurora feature should be used?

choices.text: Standard automated backups copied manually to another Region
Aurora Global Database, which replicates data to secondary Regions with typical replication lag under one second and supports fast promotion of a secondary Region to full read/write during a disaster
Cross-Region read replicas using standard MySQL asynchronous replication with 15-minute snapshot exports
Aurora Serverless v2 auto-pause

explanation: Aurora Global Database is purpose-built for cross-Region DR, using dedicated infrastructure for storage-based replication with typically sub-second lag and a documented fast promotion path for the secondary cluster during a disaster. Manual backup copies have a much larger RPO measured in hours, not seconds.

stem: A firm runs 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations and wants identical VPC, logging, and IAM guardrail resources deployed to every current and future account in specific OUs, with updates rolled out centrally. Which approach best meets this?

choices.text: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions targeting the OUs
A single CloudFormation stack deployed manually in each account
AWS Config rules with auto-remediation in each account
A Lambda function triggered by account creation that calls the CloudFormation API in each account

explanation: StackSets with service-managed permissions integrates with Organizations to automatically deploy and update stacks across accounts and OUs, including new accounts. Manual per-account stacks (B) do not scale or centralize updates, and a custom Lambda solution (D) reinvents what StackSets already provides.

stem: A team's CodePipeline deploys a CloudFormation stack to a production account from a pipeline in a shared tooling account. Deployments must not grant the pipeline broad IAM permissions in production. What should they configure?

choices.text: Have the pipeline assume a cross-account IAM role scoped to only the actions CloudFormation needs, and use a CloudFormation service role in the target account
Grant the pipeline's IAM role AdministratorAccess in the production account
Store production account root credentials in Secrets Manager for the pipeline to use
Run the pipeline directly inside the production account instead of the tooling account

explanation: Cross-account roles with a scoped CloudFormation service role enforce least privilege while still allowing centralized cross-account deployment. Granting admin access (B) or using root credentials (C) violates least privilege and security best practices.

stem: A CodeBuild project's build stage takes 25 minutes because it reinstalls all dependencies from scratch on every build, slowing the CI/CD pipeline significantly. What is the most effective way to reduce build time?

choices.text: Enable CodeBuild caching for the dependency directories in S3 or local caching
Increase the CodeBuild compute type to the largest available
Split the pipeline into more parallel CodePipeline stages
Switch from CodeBuild to running the build on a persistent EC2 instance

explanation: Caching dependency directories avoids redundant downloads/installs on each build, directly reducing build time. Increasing compute size (B) helps CPU-bound tasks but not I/O-bound dependency installation.

stem: A CloudFormation stack update fails partway through and CloudFormation automatically begins rolling back, but the rollback itself fails, leaving the stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. What is the correct next step?

choices.text: Use the ContinueUpdateRollback API/console action, skipping the resources that cannot be rolled back
Delete the stack and manually recreate all resources
Wait for CloudFormation to retry the rollback automatically
Edit the resource states directly in the AWS console to match the template

explanation: ContinueUpdateRollback lets you skip resources causing the rollback failure so the stack returns to a stable state, then remediate those resources separately. Deleting the stack (B) risks unnecessary data loss for resources not causing the issue.

stem: An architect is designing a deployment strategy for a new microservice on ECS Fargate that must shift traffic gradually to a new task set and automatically roll back on CloudWatch alarm triggers, with minimal custom scripting.

choices.text: CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for ECS with linear traffic shifting and alarm-based rollback
Manually update the ECS service desired count and monitor logs
Use a rolling update deployment configuration in the ECS service directly with no CodeDeploy integration
Deploy a new ECS cluster entirely and manually redirect Route 53 records

explanation: CodeDeploy's ECS blue/green integration natively supports linear/canary traffic shifting and automatic rollback tied to CloudWatch alarms with no custom scripting. A basic rolling update (C) lacks controlled traffic shifting and automated alarm-based rollback.

stem: A company wants to give developers self-service access to provision pre-approved, standardized architectures (e.g., a three-tier web app stack) without giving them direct IAM permissions to create arbitrary resources.

choices.text: AWS Service Catalog with CloudFormation product templates
Grant developers IAM permissions scoped to CloudFormation CreateStack only
Give developers read-only console access and have them file tickets
Systems Manager Automation documents shared publicly

explanation: Service Catalog lets administrators publish curated CloudFormation-based products that developers can launch through a constrained self-service portal, enforcing governance. Broad CreateStack permissions (B) would allow arbitrary, unapproved resource creation.

stem: A healthcare company must retain copies of critical S3 objects in a separate AWS Region for regulatory business continuity purposes, with replication of new objects happening automatically and asynchronously.

choices.text: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR)
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Same-Region Replication (SRR) only
Manually run the AWS CLI sync command nightly

explanation: S3 CRR automatically and asynchronously replicates objects to a bucket in a different region, satisfying the regulatory cross-region durability requirement. SRR (C) replicates within the same region and does not address cross-region continuity.

stem: Two AWS accounts, Account A (data producer) and Account B (analytics consumer), need Account B's IAM role to read objects from an S3 bucket owned by Account A, following least-privilege principles.

choices.text: Attach a bucket policy in Account A granting the specific Account B IAM role read access, with no additional cross-account IAM policy required on the bucket owner's side beyond that
Make the bucket public and rely on obscurity of the bucket name for security
Create a duplicate copy of the data in Account B daily via manual export
Grant Account B's root user full access to Account A via IAM
Only apply an IAM policy in Account B without any bucket policy in Account A

explanation: A bucket policy in the resource-owning account explicitly naming the consuming account's role is the standard, least-privilege method for cross-account S3 access. Relying solely on an IAM policy in the consuming account (E) is insufficient because the resource owner must also grant access via a resource-based policy.

stem: A company wants RDS database credentials rotated automatically every 30 days without requiring application downtime or manual password updates in application configuration.

choices.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled using the built-in RDS rotation Lambda function
Store the credentials in Systems Manager Parameter Store as SecureString with no rotation configured
Hardcode credentials in an encrypted configuration file redeployed manually each month
Rotate the RDS master password manually via the console every 30 days

explanation: Secrets Manager provides built-in Lambda rotation functions specifically for RDS that update both the database and the secret transparently, with applications retrieving the current value at runtime. Parameter Store SecureString (B) does not include native automatic rotation functionality.

stem: An Auto Scaling group backs an API whose CPU utilization fluctuates unpredictably. The team wants the group to automatically maintain CPU utilization near a specific target value without manually defining scaling thresholds or step adjustments.

choices.text: Target tracking scaling policy based on average CPU utilization
Step scaling policy with multiple CloudWatch alarm thresholds
Simple scaling policy with a single alarm
Scheduled scaling actions based on time of day

explanation: Target tracking automatically calculates and adjusts capacity to keep a metric like CPU utilization near a target value, without manually configured thresholds. Step scaling (B) requires manually defined alarm thresholds and adjustment steps.

stem: An Auto Scaling group terminates instances during scale-in, but the application needs time to gracefully deregister from a service registry and flush in-flight requests before termination completes. What should be configured?

choices.text: An Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on the terminating state to delay termination while cleanup logic runs
A longer health check grace period on the Auto Scaling group
A larger cooldown period between scaling activities
Termination protection enabled on all instances

explanation: Lifecycle hooks pause an instance in a wait state during launch or termination, giving custom code time to complete tasks like deregistration before the instance is actually terminated. The health check grace period (B) only affects when health checks start being evaluated after launch, not termination behavior.

stem: Users report intermittent slow response times on a distributed microservices application, but aggregate CloudWatch metrics show no obvious single bottleneck. The team needs to pinpoint which specific service call in a request chain is causing latency.

choices.text: Enable AWS X-Ray tracing across the services to analyze the service map and trace segment latencies
Increase CloudWatch metric resolution to 1-second granularity only
Enable VPC Flow Logs and manually correlate timestamps
Add more CloudWatch alarms on CPU utilization

explanation: X-Ray provides distributed tracing across microservices, visualizing a service map and per-segment latency to pinpoint the exact call causing delays. VPC Flow Logs (C) show network flow metadata, not application-level request tracing.

stem: A high-traffic application uses DynamoDB as its primary data store and needs microsecond read latency for a small set of extremely hot keys accessed millions of times per minute, beyond what DynamoDB alone typically delivers.

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached placed in front of DynamoDB manually with custom cache invalidation logic as the only viable option
DynamoDB Global Tables
DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode alone

explanation: DAX is a DynamoDB-native, write-through caching layer purpose-built to deliver microsecond read latency for DynamoDB without application-managed cache invalidation logic. A generic ElastiCache layer (B) would work but requires substantially more custom cache-management code than the purpose-built DAX.

stem: A company wants a centralized, policy-driven backup solution across EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS resources spanning multiple AWS accounts, with backups copied to a separate, logically isolated backup account to protect against ransomware or accidental account compromise. Which approach best meets this?

choices.text: Configure each service's native automated snapshot feature individually in every account
Use AWS Backup with an organization-wide backup policy managed through AWS Organizations, with cross-account backup copy into a dedicated backup account's vault protected by a vault lock
Use AWS DataSync to copy nightly backups into another account's S3 bucket
Rely on the default 7-day RDS automated backup retention alone

explanation: AWS Backup provides centralized, cross-service, cross-account and cross-region backup orchestration, and Backup Vault Lock adds immutability that directly addresses ransomware and account-compromise isolation concerns. Configuring per-service native snapshots does not centralize management, and DataSync is designed for data transfer, not managed backup lifecycle across these AWS services.

stem: A European company must ensure that no S3 buckets or RDS instances are ever created outside the eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 Regions across its entire AWS Organization, to satisfy a data residency requirement. The company wants to prevent the action rather than merely detect it afterward. What should they implement?

choices.text: An AWS Config rule that flags noncompliant Regions after resources are created
A service control policy attached at the organizational unit level that denies the relevant API calls when the aws:RequestedRegion condition key does not match the two approved Regions
An EventBridge rule that automatically deletes noncompliant resources after creation
An IAM permissions boundary applied per user restricting allowed Regions

explanation: A service control policy can deny API calls organization-wide based on the aws:RequestedRegion condition key, providing preventive enforcement before a noncompliant resource is ever created, which directly satisfies the 'prevent rather than detect' requirement. AWS Config and an after-the-fact deletion rule are detective and reactive controls, not preventive ones.

stem: As part of a migration to a multi-account AWS Organizations structure, a company wants its 2,000 employees to sign in once using their existing on-premises Active Directory credentials and access multiple AWS accounts and roles without managing separate IAM users in each account. Which approach should they implement?

choices.text: Set up AWS IAM Identity Center, integrated with the existing Active Directory via AD Connector or a trust with AWS Managed Microsoft AD, to provide centralized single sign-on and permission sets across all Organizations accounts
Create individual IAM users with the same password in every AWS account
Use Amazon Cognito user pools federated independently per account
Manually configure a separate SAML identity provider trust in each of the 2,000 employees' target accounts

explanation: IAM Identity Center is purpose-built for centralized workforce single sign-on across an AWS Organizations multi-account structure, integrating with on-premises AD via AD Connector or an AWS Managed Microsoft AD trust and assigning permission sets per account. Duplicating IAM users, using Cognito (built for application end-user identity), or configuring per-account SAML trusts manually do not scale for this use case.

stem: A team migrating a set of containerized batch-processing jobs wants to avoid managing, patching, and scaling EC2 instances for their ECS cluster, and is willing to accept less control over the underlying compute environment in exchange for per-task billing. Which ECS launch type should they choose?

choices.text: AWS Fargate launch type
EC2 launch type with manual Auto Scaling
EC2 launch type using Spot Instances only
ECS Anywhere running on on-premises infrastructure

explanation: The Fargate launch type removes the need to provision or manage underlying EC2 instances, billing per task based on vCPU and memory consumed, at the cost of less low-level control over the host environment. The EC2 launch type, with or without Spot, still requires managing instances, and ECS Anywhere runs tasks on customer-managed on-premises infrastructure, which does not fit this cloud-migration goal.

stem: A company uses AWS CodePipeline with a deploy stage in a different AWS Region than the pipeline itself. The pipeline's artifact S3 bucket is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. After adding the cross-region deploy stage, the pipeline fails with an access denied error when the deploy stage tries to read the artifact. What is the most likely cause and correct fix?

choices.text: CodePipeline requires a separate artifact store (S3 bucket plus KMS key) defined for each region used by the pipeline, and the KMS key policy for the target region's key must grant decrypt permission to the CodePipeline service role and any deploy-side roles.
Enable S3 cross-region replication on the artifact bucket instead of defining a per-region artifact store.
Switch the artifact bucket encryption to SSE-S3 (AES256) since KMS keys cannot be used across regions.
Grant the deploy stage's IAM role s3:GetObject only; KMS permissions are not required for cross-region artifact access.

explanation: Cross-region actions in CodePipeline require you to configure a separate regional artifact store (bucket and KMS key) for each region, and the KMS key policy must explicitly grant decrypt permissions to the roles involved. Simply granting S3 permissions without KMS decrypt (D) or relying on S3 replication (B) does not satisfy CodePipeline's cross-region artifact store requirements.

stem: A CodeBuild project needs to connect to an RDS MySQL database during integration tests. The security team requires that database credentials be rotated automatically every 30 days without requiring changes to the buildspec each time. Which approach meets this requirement with the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled using the RDS rotation function, and reference the secret ARN in the CodeBuild project's environment variable configuration with type SECRETS_MANAGER.
Store the credentials as SecureString parameters in SSM Parameter Store and manually update them every 30 days using a scheduled Lambda function you build yourself.
Hardcode the credentials as plaintext environment variables in buildspec.yml and update the file every 30 days.
Store the credentials in a private S3 bucket and download them at build time using an IAM role.

explanation: Secrets Manager provides native, managed rotation for RDS credentials, and CodeBuild can reference a secret directly as an environment variable of type SECRETS_MANAGER so builds always retrieve the current value with no buildspec changes. Option B requires building and maintaining custom rotation logic instead of using a managed capability.

stem: A DevOps team is migrating source repositories from AWS CodeCommit to GitHub and needs CodePipeline to trigger automatically on every push to the main branch with minimal latency and without storing long-lived GitHub credentials in AWS. Which source action configuration should they use?

choices.text: Configure the source stage with the GitHub Version 1 source action using a personal access token stored as a pipeline parameter.
Configure the source stage with a CodeStar Connections (GitHub) source action, which uses a managed OAuth-based connection and triggers via a webhook.
Configure the source stage to poll GitHub periodically using CodePipeline's default polling mechanism.
Set up a scheduled EventBridge rule that calls StartPipelineExecution every 5 minutes.

explanation: CodeStar Connections provides a secure, managed OAuth-based integration with GitHub with no long-lived credentials stored in AWS, and it triggers pipeline executions near-instantly via webhook. Polling (C) and scheduled polling workarounds (D) add latency, and the V1 GitHub action (A) requires storing a personal access token.

stem: An organization needs to store database connection strings used by multiple CodeBuild projects. Some values are static configuration that rarely changes and does not need automatic rotation, while others are credentials that must rotate every 90 days with built-in rotation support. Which combination minimizes cost while meeting these requirements?

choices.text: Store all values in AWS Secrets Manager, since it is the only service that supports encryption at rest.
Store the static configuration in SSM Parameter Store (standard tier, SecureString) and the rotating credentials in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation configured.
Store all values in SSM Parameter Store advanced tier and write custom Lambda functions to rotate everything on a schedule.
Store all values as encrypted environment variables directly in the CodeBuild project definition.

explanation: Parameter Store SecureString (standard tier) is free and well suited to static configuration, while Secrets Manager's built-in rotation workflows justify its additional cost only for credentials that need periodic rotation. Using Secrets Manager for everything (A) increases cost unnecessarily since Parameter Store also encrypts values at rest.

stem: A CodePipeline for a production deployment must pause after the staging deployment stage and require sign-off from a release manager before proceeding to production, with an email notification sent when approval is pending. How should this be implemented?

choices.text: Add a Manual Approval action between the staging and production stages, and configure an SNS topic on that action so subscribers are notified when the pipeline reaches it.
Add a Lambda invoke action that pauses the pipeline for a fixed 24-hour period before continuing.
Configure the production CodeDeploy application to require a CloudFormation change set review.
Replace CodePipeline with AWS Step Functions to add a wait state before the production stage.

explanation: CodePipeline's Manual Approval action natively halts execution until approved or rejected and can publish to an SNS topic to notify reviewers. Options B and D reimplement native functionality with less reliability and more operational overhead.

stem: A CodeBuild project that runs integration tests against a private RDS instance was working correctly, but after increasing the number of concurrent builds it began intermittently failing with connection timeouts. The project runs inside a VPC using a dedicated /28 subnet. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The RDS security group does not allow inbound traffic from the CodeBuild security group.
Each concurrent CodeBuild build consumes an ENI in the subnet, and the small /28 CIDR block runs out of available IP addresses under increased concurrency.
CodeBuild does not support VPC connectivity for concurrent builds.
The RDS instance's maximum connection limit has been reached due to a CodeBuild security group misconfiguration.

explanation: Every CodeBuild build running in a VPC allocates its own ENI in the configured subnet; a /28 subnet has very few usable IP addresses, so scaling concurrency exhausts them and causes intermittent failures under load. A security group misconfiguration (A) would cause consistent failures regardless of load, not intermittent ones tied to concurrency.

stem: A DevOps engineer is writing an AppSpec file for a CodeDeploy EC2/on-premises deployment that must stop the running application, prepare and install the new revision, install dependencies, start the application, and finally validate that it responds on its health endpoint. In which order should these lifecycle event hooks appear?

choices.text: ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService
BeforeInstall, ApplicationStop, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService
ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ValidateService, ApplicationStart
ApplicationStart, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStop, ValidateService

explanation: The CodeDeploy EC2/on-premises lifecycle proceeds ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, (Install), AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService, so hooks run in that sequence relative to the reserved Install step. Option B incorrectly places BeforeInstall ahead of ApplicationStop, and C runs ValidateService before the application has even started.

stem: A team currently runs Jenkins on self-managed EC2 instances and wants to migrate to a fully managed AWS-native CI/CD solution to reduce operational overhead, while keeping their existing test logic with minimal rework. Which migration approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Replace Jenkins with CodeBuild and CodePipeline, translating the existing pipeline logic into buildspec.yml commands and CodePipeline stages for source, build, test, and deploy.
Keep Jenkins as the orchestrator but simply run the Jenkins controller inside a CodeBuild container with no other changes.
Migrate directly to standalone AWS Lambda functions to replace every Jenkins pipeline stage.
Use AWS CodeStar to automatically convert Jenkinsfiles into CodePipeline definitions without any modification.

explanation: Migrating to CodeBuild/CodePipeline requires translating existing pipeline logic into buildspec commands and pipeline stage definitions; there is no automated Jenkinsfile-to-CodePipeline conversion capability, making D incorrect. Running Jenkins inside CodeBuild (B) does not actually achieve a managed-service migration.

stem: After a security team applies a new IAM permissions boundary to all CI/CD service roles, a CodeBuild project that previously deployed CloudFormation stacks starts failing with AccessDenied on cloudformation:CreateStack, even though the CodeBuild service role's attached policy still includes that permission. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The permissions boundary does not include cloudformation:CreateStack among its allowed actions, and effective permissions are the intersection of the role's policy and the boundary, denying the action.
Permissions boundaries only apply to IAM users, not roles, so this cannot be the cause.
CodeBuild ignores IAM permissions boundaries entirely.
The buildspec.yml file must explicitly list every IAM action the build will perform.

explanation: A permissions boundary caps the maximum permissions a role can have; the role's effective permissions are the intersection of its identity policy and the boundary, so an action absent from the boundary is denied even if the attached policy allows it. Boundaries apply to roles as well as users, making B false.

stem: A platform team supports dozens of application teams that each need an identical CI/CD pipeline structure that must be version-controlled, code-reviewed, and easily replicated for new microservices. What approach best achieves this at scale?

choices.text: Manually create each pipeline through the CodePipeline console and document the steps in a runbook for consistency.
Define the pipeline structure as a reusable CloudFormation or CDK template, store it in version control, and have each team instantiate a stack from it with team-specific parameters.
Use AWS Config rules to enforce that pipelines have identical stage names after they are created.
Export each existing pipeline's JSON definition via the CLI and manually copy-paste it for new teams.

explanation: Pipeline-as-code using CloudFormation or CDK enables version control, code review, and consistent, repeatable provisioning of pipeline infrastructure across many teams. Manual console creation (A) and copy-pasted JSON (D) do not scale and are error-prone.

stem: A team needs to store over 15,000 configuration parameters, some larger than 4 KB, and requires higher API throughput than the default standard-tier limit allows. Which SSM Parameter Store configuration should they use?

choices.text: Standard tier parameters only, since Parameter Store has no limit on total parameter count or throughput.
Advanced tier parameters, which support larger values, a higher total parameter quota per account, and optionally higher throughput.
Migrate everything to Secrets Manager since Parameter Store cannot exceed 10,000 parameters under any configuration.
Use standard tier but request an AWS Support limit increase, since parameter value size cannot be changed regardless of tier.

explanation: Advanced tier parameters support larger values than standard tier, raise the account's total parameter quota, and can be configured for higher throughput, directly addressing both stated needs. Standard tier has lower default limits that would be exceeded here, making A incorrect.

stem: A CodePipeline currently uses the default EventBridge-based trigger for its CodeCommit source stage. During a migration, an engineer temporarily reverts the source action to periodic polling. What tradeoff does this introduce?

choices.text: No tradeoff; polling and event-based triggers behave identically in every respect.

Polling introduces added latency, since executions only start at the polling interval, and can generate more API calls, whereas the event-based trigger starts execution almost immediately after a change is detected.
Polling is inherently more secure because it does not rely on EventBridge rules.
Polling eliminates cost entirely, while event-based triggers always incur charges.

explanation: EventBridge-based change detection starts a pipeline execution almost immediately after a source change, while polling checks on a fixed interval, adding latency and unnecessary API calls when nothing changed. There is no inherent security or cost advantage to polling as described in C and D.

stem: A team practicing continuous delivery wants every commit to main to be automatically buildable and potentially releasable, while minimizing long-lived feature branches that cause painful merge conflicts. Which source control and pipeline strategy best supports this goal?

choices.text: GitFlow, with separate long-lived develop, release, and hotfix branches, each triggering its own pipeline.

Trunk-based development, where small, frequent changes merge into a single main branch protected by required CodeBuild status checks on pull requests, and every merge to main triggers the CI/CD pipeline.
Feature branches left open for months until a feature is fully complete, then merged directly to production without CI checks.
A single shared branch with no pull request or automated build gating, relying on manual review over email.

explanation: Trunk-based development with short-lived branches and mandatory automated checks on every merge is the standard practice enabling continuous delivery and fast, low-conflict integration. GitFlow's long-lived branches (A) delay integration and increase merge complexity, working against the stated goal.

stem: A team wants pull requests opened against their main branch in a GitHub-hosted repository to automatically trigger a CodeBuild project running unit tests, and wants the PR blocked from merging if tests fail, without running a full CodePipeline execution for every PR. Which approach satisfies this?

choices.text: Configure CodePipeline to poll for new pull requests and run a full pipeline execution for each one.

Configure a CodeBuild webhook filter group for PULL_REQUEST_CREATED and PULL_REQUEST_UPDATED events, and require the resulting CodeBuild status check to pass in GitHub branch protection settings before merging.
Manually trigger CodeBuild builds after each pull request is opened.
Use CodeDeploy's ApplicationStart lifecycle hook on a test EC2 instance to run the unit tests.

explanation: CodeBuild supports webhook filter groups that trigger builds directly on GitHub pull request events, and GitHub branch protection can require that status check before merge, avoiding the overhead of a full pipeline per PR. CodeDeploy lifecycle hooks (D) apply to deployments, not to gating PR merges.

stem: A DevOps team must add static application security testing to their pipeline so builds fail automatically when high-severity vulnerabilities are found in application code, before the artifact is published to the artifact repository. How should this be implemented?

choices.text: Add a post-build phase that runs the SAST tool and manually reviews the results after the pipeline has already completed.

Add a dedicated build phase in the CodeBuild buildspec that runs the SAST tool, parses its output, and exits with a non-zero status when high-severity findings exist, failing the phase before the artifact is published.
Run the SAST scan only in the production environment after deployment.
Use Amazon Macie to scan the application source code for security vulnerabilities.

explanation: Configuring the buildspec to exit non-zero on high-severity SAST findings halts the pipeline before the artifact is published, enforcing a true security gate. Amazon Macie (D) discovers sensitive data in S3 and is not designed for source code vulnerability scanning.

stem: Before promoting a new microservice version to production, a team needs to run a load test simulating 10,000 concurrent users against staging and automatically fail the pipeline if p99 latency exceeds an SLA. Which pipeline design best achieves this?

choices.text: Add a manual step where an engineer runs load tests locally and reports the results verbally before approving production deployment.

Add a stage that runs a distributed load test against the staging endpoint, publishes p99 latency as a CloudWatch custom metric, and add a subsequent check (via Lambda or a CloudWatch alarm) that fails the pipeline if the SLA is breached.
Rely solely on CodeDeploy's ValidateService hook during production deployment to perform the load test.
Skip load testing in the pipeline and monitor production traffic patterns after release instead.

explanation: Running load tests in an automated stage with results published to CloudWatch and gated by a threshold check integrates performance validation directly into the pipeline before production promotion. Testing only in production after release (D) fails to catch issues before they affect users.

stem: A CodeDeploy deployment to an Auto Scaling group must confirm that the newly deployed version responds successfully on its /health endpoint before CodeDeploy considers the deployment successful on each instance. Which lifecycle hook should contain this check, and what happens if it fails?

choices.text: The check belongs in BeforeInstall; if it fails, CodeDeploy skips that instance but continues on the others.

The check belongs in ValidateService; if the script exits non-zero, CodeDeploy marks that instance's deployment as failed, which, depending on configuration, can halt or roll back the overall deployment.
The check belongs in ApplicationStop, run before the old version is removed.
Health checks cannot be customized in CodeDeploy; only the built-in ELB health check can be used.

explanation: ValidateService is the final lifecycle event intended to confirm a deployment succeeded; a non-zero exit fails that instance's deployment and, depending on the deployment configuration and failure thresholds, can trigger rollback. BeforeInstall (A) runs before the new version is even started, so it cannot validate the new version's health.

stem: A team wants to add a custom acceptance test step to CodePipeline that isn't supported by any built-in action type, such as calling an internal test orchestration API and waiting for a pass/fail verdict. How can this be integrated?

choices.text: It cannot be done; CodePipeline only supports its built-in action types.
Add a Lambda invoke action whose function calls the external API and reports success or failure back to CodePipeline using PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult.
Add a manual approval action and have a human run the acceptance tests instead.
Publish to an SNS topic to trigger the acceptance tests asynchronously with no way to gate the pipeline on the outcome.

explanation: A Lambda invoke action lets custom code participate in a stage, and the function must call PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult to tell CodePipeline whether to proceed, enabling arbitrary custom integrations. Option A is false since Lambda invoke actions exist specifically for this kind of extensibility.

stem: A QA team wants to run Selenium-based UI acceptance tests against a freshly deployed staging environment as part of the pipeline, requiring a headless browser and specific driver versions. What is the most appropriate way to run these tests in CodeBuild?

choices.text: Use the default CodeBuild managed image and rely on manually installed browser software cached between unrelated builds.

Use a custom CodeBuild Docker image that includes the required browser and driver versions, reference it in the project configuration, and run the Selenium suite as a build phase against the staging URL.
Run Selenium tests only on a developer's local machine and paste screenshots into the pipeline's approval action.
Selenium tests cannot run in CodeBuild because it does not support headless browser execution.

explanation: CodeBuild's support for custom build images is the standard approach for including specific browser and driver versions needed for Selenium-based UI testing, run as a build phase in the buildspec. Option D is incorrect since headless browsers run fine inside CodeBuild containers.

stem: A pipeline's integration test stage intermittently fails with data conflicts, and investigation shows multiple concurrent pipeline executions from different feature branches all run tests against the same shared RDS test database, causing race conditions. What is the best long-term fix?

choices.text: Increase the RDS instance size to handle more concurrent connections.

Provision an ephemeral, isolated test database or schema per pipeline execution (for example, via a temporary snapshot restore or containerized database) and tear it down after the test stage completes.
Serialize all pipeline executions so only one runs at a time across the entire organization.
Disable integration tests and rely solely on unit tests going forward.

explanation: Isolating test data per execution eliminates cross-execution race conditions without sacrificing parallel pipeline throughput. Serializing every execution (C) severely limits throughput and does not scale, and removing integration tests (D) reduces overall quality assurance.

stem: A team wants CodeBuild to natively aggregate and display JUnit XML test results, including pass/fail counts and trends over time, in the AWS console without writing custom parsing scripts. Which CodeBuild feature should they configure?

choices.text: CodeBuild build badges
CodeBuild test reports, configured via a reports section in buildspec.yml pointing to the JUnit XML output files, producing a report group with historical trends in the console.
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries against the raw build log output.
AWS X-Ray annotations added to the buildspec.

explanation: CodeBuild's built-in test reporting ingests JUnit/Cucumber/NUnit-format XML files referenced in the buildspec's reports section and renders pass/fail summaries and trends natively. Build badges (A) only show overall build status, not detailed per-test results.

stem: A team is deciding whether to run unit tests within the same CodeBuild project's build phase (before the artifact is fully packaged) or as a separate CodePipeline stage after the build stage produces artifacts. What is the key tradeoff?

choices.text: Running tests within the build phase gives faster fail-fast feedback and avoids packaging artifacts that will fail anyway, but mixes test and build logs; a separate stage isolates concerns and can reuse the built artifact across multiple test types at the cost of extra stage transition latency.
There is no meaningful difference; CodePipeline stages and CodeBuild phases behave identically in execution time.
Unit tests must always run after deployment to a live environment, so neither option described is valid.
Running tests before packaging the artifact is technically impossible in CodeBuild.

explanation: Testing earlier in the build gives faster feedback and avoids wasted compute on doomed builds, while a separate post-build stage enables reuse of one built artifact across multiple parallel test types at the cost of added stage latency. Neither ordering is impossible, so C and D are incorrect.

stem: A company uses a third-party SaaS security scanning service that requires submitting a build artifact, then polling for a scan result that can take up to 20 minutes. Which pipeline design handles this long-running asynchronous external call most robustly?

choices.text: Add a CodeBuild phase that submits the scan and then sleeps in a polling loop for up to 20 minutes within the same build.
Add a Lambda invoke action that submits the scan job and immediately reports success, ignoring the eventual result.

Use a Lambda invoke action (or Step Functions) that submits the scan request and, via a separate polling mechanism, calls PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult only once the real verdict is available, so the stage genuinely waits for the outcome.
Skip automated integration and have a security engineer manually check the SaaS dashboard after every deployment.

explanation: The CodePipeline Lambda job-worker pattern (or Step Functions) is designed for long-running asynchronous external calls, reporting success or failure only once the real result is known, rather than blocking build compute for 20 minutes (A) or falsely reporting success immediately (B).

stem: A team wants to continuously verify that key user-facing API endpoints remain within acceptable latency thresholds after every production deployment, using synthetic transactions run on an ongoing schedule rather than only during pipeline execution. Which AWS capability is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: AWS CodeBuild scheduled builds
Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries, which run configurable scripts on a schedule against live endpoints and publish latency and availability metrics with alarming support.
AWS CodeDeploy ValidateService hooks, which only run once at deployment time.
AWS X-Ray sampling rules.

explanation: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries are designed for scheduled, ongoing synthetic monitoring of live endpoints, publishing metrics that can drive alarms independent of any specific deployment event. ValidateService (C) only executes during the deployment lifecycle, not continuously afterward.

stem: A team wants pull requests in their CodeCommit-based workflow to automatically receive code quality and security recommendations, with the ability to block merges when critical issues are found. How should this be integrated?

choices.text: Associate the CodeCommit repository with Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer so it automatically posts recommendations on pull requests, and add a CodeBuild step that queries the CodeGuru Reviewer API for open critical recommendations, failing the build (and required status check) if any exist.
Manually copy code into the CodeGuru console before every pull request.
CodeGuru Reviewer only works with GitHub repositories, so this cannot be done with CodeCommit.
Use CodeGuru Profiler to analyze pull request code changes for security issues.

explanation: CodeGuru Reviewer supports CodeCommit repository associations and automatically comments on pull requests, and its API can be queried to gate merges via a required CodeBuild status check. CodeGuru Profiler (D) analyzes runtime performance, not static PR code review.

stem: A pipeline deploys to dev, staging, and production environments requiring different test depths: dev runs only unit tests; staging runs unit, integration, and load tests; production should proceed only if staging's tests and a security scan passed. How should the pipeline be structured to enforce this?

choices.text: Run all test types once at the very beginning of the pipeline, before any deployment stage, and treat the result as valid for every environment.
Structure the pipeline with sequential stages per environment, each containing its required test and scan actions, so promotion only occurs when all actions in the prior stage(s) succeed.
Deploy to all three environments in parallel and roll back any environment that later fails its tests.
Use a single environment for dev, staging, and production, distinguished only by feature flags, eliminating the need for separate test stages.

explanation: CodePipeline's sequential stage model enforces gating naturally: a stage only proceeds when all of its actions succeed, so placing environment-appropriate tests and scans in each stage ensures production is reached only after staging validation passes. Testing once upfront (A) does not validate the actual staging-deployed build, and parallel deployment (C) risks exposing untested code to production.

stem: A company wants to use approved internal versions of npm and Maven packages while still allowing developers to pull from the public npmjs and Maven Central registries when an internal version isn't yet available, all through a single centrally managed endpoint. Which AWS CodeArtifact configuration achieves this?

choices.text: Create separate, unconnected CodeArtifact repositories for internal and public packages, requiring developers to manually choose which to query.

Create a CodeArtifact repository with an external connection to the public npm/Maven registries configured as an upstream, and chain internal package repositories as additional upstreams, so one endpoint serves both, with internal packages taking precedence.
Use S3 buckets directly as the package registry instead of CodeArtifact.
CodeArtifact does not support connecting to public package registries; a VPN link to npmjs.com is required.

explanation: CodeArtifact supports chaining upstream repositories, including public registries like npmjs and Maven Central, alongside internal repositories, so a single downstream endpoint can serve both consistently. Option D is factually wrong since public upstream connections are a native CodeArtifact feature.

stem: A security team wants continuous vulnerability scanning of container images in Amazon ECR that keeps rescanning images as new CVE data becomes available, not just a one-time scan at push. Which ECR scanning configuration should they enable?

choices.text: Basic scanning, which scans an image once at push time using a static CVE database.
Enhanced scanning, powered by Amazon Inspector, which continuously and automatically rescans images for OS and select language package vulnerabilities as new CVE data is published.
Manually re-push each image daily to trigger a fresh basic scan.
Amazon Macie image scanning.

explanation: Enhanced scanning integrates with Amazon Inspector to continuously monitor and rescan ECR images against updated CVE data, whereas basic scanning only scans once at push using a static ruleset. Macie (D) is unrelated to container image vulnerability scanning.

stem: An incident occurred when a teammate overwrote the prod tag in ECR with an unintended image, causing a deployment to pull the wrong image. How can this specific class of incident be prevented going forward?

choices.text: Enable image tag immutability on the ECR repository so no tag can be overwritten once pushed, forcing a new unique tag or digest for every push.
Enable ECR lifecycle policies to delete old images automatically.
Enable enhanced scanning on the repository.
Require that all ECR pushes go through a CodeBuild project, which alone prevents tag overwrites.

explanation: ECR's image tag immutability setting directly prevents overwriting an existing tag, which is exactly the failure mode described. Routing pushes through CodeBuild (D) does not by itself prevent tag overwrites unless combined with immutability or unique tagging conventions.

stem: A CodePipeline's S3 artifact bucket has grown to several terabytes because artifacts from every execution over the past two years are retained, increasing storage cost with no compliance requirement to keep them that long. How can costs be reduced while retaining recent artifacts needed for troubleshooting?

choices.text: Delete the S3 bucket and recreate it, losing all artifact history immediately.

Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy that transitions older artifacts to a lower-cost storage class after a set period and expires artifacts beyond a defined retention window, balancing cost against troubleshooting needs.
Move all artifacts to Amazon EFS instead of S3.
Disable artifact storage entirely so CodePipeline stops producing S3 objects.

explanation: S3 Lifecycle policies automatically transition aging objects to cheaper storage classes and expire them after a retention period, directly addressing cost while preserving recent artifacts. CodePipeline requires an S3 artifact store to function, so disabling it (D) is not viable.

stem: A company wants to produce hardened, patched golden AMIs on a recurring schedule that incorporate the latest OS security patches, run automated tests against the resulting AMI, and distribute the validated AMI to multiple accounts and regions. Which service is purpose-built for this workflow?

choices.text: AWS CodeBuild alone, using a custom script that calls the CreateImage API.

EC2 Image Builder, which provides a pipeline to automate building, testing via test components, and distributing AMIs or container images on a schedule, including cross-account and cross-region distribution.
AWS CodeDeploy, using an AppSpec file to define AMI creation steps.
Amazon ECR, configured with a lifecycle policy to rebuild AMIs periodically.

explanation: EC2 Image Builder is the dedicated service for automating creation, testing, and multi-account/multi-region distribution of golden AMIs and container images on a schedule. ECR (D) is a container registry and has no AMI-building capability.

stem: A team's Lambda function requires several large ML libraries, pushing the deployment package size close to the zipped package limit. They want a packaging approach supporting significantly larger dependencies that integrates with their existing container-based CI/CD tooling. What should they do?

choices.text: Continue using a .zip deployment package but request an AWS Support limit increase, since the zip size limit can be raised for any account.
Package the function as a container image, stored in Amazon ECR and up to 10 GB, and configure the Lambda function to use that image instead of a .zip package.
Split the function into 50 smaller Lambda functions to stay under the zip limit.
Move the workload to AWS Batch, since Lambda cannot support ML libraries under any packaging model.

explanation: Lambda supports container image packaging up to 10 GB, far larger than zipped deployment package limits, accommodating large dependencies and integrating naturally with Docker-based CI/CD via ECR. The zip package size limit (A) is a hard limit that cannot be raised via a support request.

stem: A central platform team manages a CodeArtifact domain and repository that must be consumed by CodeBuild projects in dozens of separate accounts within an AWS Organization, without duplicating the repository or granting account-level admin access. What is the recommended way to enable this?

choices.text: Manually copy the CodeArtifact repository contents to an S3 bucket in each consuming account.
Attach a resource policy to the CodeArtifact domain and/or repository granting the specific actions needed (such as GetAuthorizationToken and ReadFromRepository) to the consuming accounts or roles.
Grant each consuming account's CodeBuild role AdministratorAccess in the platform account.
CodeArtifact repositories cannot be shared across accounts; each account must maintain its own independent repository.

explanation: CodeArtifact supports resource-based policies on domains and repositories, enabling fine-grained cross-account access to a single shared repository without duplicating data or granting broad administrative permissions. Option D is incorrect, since cross-account sharing is an explicitly supported CodeArtifact capability.

stem: An application deploys containers to ECS clusters in both us-east-1 and eu-west-1, and the team wants images pushed to ECR in us-east-1 to automatically become available in eu-west-1 without a manual push step, minimizing pull latency for eu-west-1 clusters. What ECR feature should they configure?

choices.text: Cross-region replication configured on the ECR private registry, which automatically copies images pushed in one region to repositories in the destination region.
A script that runs docker pull and docker push after every deployment to copy images between regions manually.
Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication, since ECR images are stored directly as customer-accessible S3 objects.
ECR does not support any form of cross-region image replication.

explanation: ECR supports registry-level cross-region (and cross-account) replication rules that automatically copy newly pushed images to specified destination regions, removing the need for manual copy steps. S3 CRR (C) does not apply since customers cannot directly manipulate ECR's underlying storage this way.

stem: A monorepo contains both a containerized backend service and a Lambda-based event processor, and a single CodeBuild project builds both on each commit. What is an appropriate buildspec design to publish both artifact types correctly?

choices.text: It is not possible for a single CodeBuild project to produce more than one type of artifact.

Define build phases that build and push the Docker image to ECR, and separately zip the Lambda code, uploading it via the CodeBuild artifacts output or directly to S3/Lambda within the buildspec, so one build publishes both artifact types.
Use CodeDeploy to build and push the Docker image, since CodeBuild cannot run Docker commands.
Split into two separate CodeCommit repositories, since a CodeBuild project can only reference one artifact repository type.

explanation: A single CodeBuild buildspec can include multiple phases that both push a Docker image to ECR and package/upload a Lambda zip artifact, enabling one build to produce multiple artifact types. CodeBuild fully supports Docker commands in privileged mode, making C incorrect.

stem: A regulated company must produce AMIs that comply with DISA STIG hardening benchmarks, with automated validation that hardening was applied correctly before an AMI is used, and this process must repeat whenever the base AMI is patched. Which approach best satisfies this using AWS-native tooling?

choices.text: Manually harden a single AMI once and reuse it indefinitely.

Use EC2 Image Builder with a hardening component in the build phase and a corresponding test component that validates compliance, running the pipeline on a recurring schedule or triggered by base image updates.
Use AWS Config rules to harden AMIs after they are launched into EC2 instances.
Use Amazon Inspector to automatically modify AMI configurations to meet STIG requirements.

explanation: EC2 Image Builder explicitly supports hardening and test components executed as part of an image pipeline, with recurring or event-based triggers keeping AMIs current and validated. AWS Config (C) can detect drift but does not build or harden AMIs, and Inspector (D) scans for vulnerabilities but does not remediate configuration.

stem: Developers report that npm install commands in CodeBuild suddenly fail to resolve certain public packages that previously worked, after the platform team added a new internal CodeArtifact repository as an additional upstream ahead of the existing public npm upstream in the dependency chain. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: CodeArtifact repositories can only have one upstream at a time, so adding a second one silently disabled the first.

The new internal repository is positioned earlier in the upstream chain but is not correctly linked through to the public registry, so resolution effectively fails before falling through to the public upstream.
npm cannot be used with CodeArtifact; only pip and Maven are supported.
CodeBuild has a hardcoded allowlist of package registries that excludes CodeArtifact.

explanation: CodeArtifact resolves packages by walking the configured upstream chain in order, so an intermediate repository that is not properly linked to the public upstream can break resolution of packages that previously worked. CodeArtifact supports multiple upstream repositories per repository, so A is false, and it fully supports npm, making C false.

stem: An ECR repository is accumulating a large number of untagged images left behind from a CI process that overwrites tags on every build, consuming storage that is never cleaned up. What is the most appropriate fix?

choices.text: Manually delete untagged images from the ECR console every week.
Configure an ECR lifecycle policy rule that expires images with untagged status after a defined age or count threshold, automatically cleaning up dangling images.
Enable ECR enhanced scanning, which automatically removes untagged images.
Switch to image tag immutability, which will automatically delete old untagged images.

explanation: ECR lifecycle policies can specifically target untagged images and expire them once an age or count threshold is exceeded, directly solving the storage accumulation problem without manual effort. Enhanced scanning (C) only scans for vulnerabilities and has no cleanup function, and immutability (D) only prevents tag overwrites.

stem: A pipeline in Account A builds container images and pushes them to a shared ECR repository, and Account B's ECS service must pull those images. The images must be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key controlled by Account A, and Account B must be able to decrypt only what is necessary to pull the image, following least privilege. What should be configured?

choices.text: Share the KMS key's full administrative permissions with Account B so it can manage the key itself.

Configure ECR repository encryption with Account A's customer-managed KMS key, update the key policy to grant Account B's ECS task execution role kms:Decrypt (and needed grant permissions), and configure an ECR repository policy allowing Account B to pull images.
Disable encryption on the repository, since cross-account KMS access is not supported for ECR.
Copy the KMS key into Account B so each account has an independent copy of the same key material.

explanation: Cross-account decryption requires granting the consuming account's role narrowly scoped kms:Decrypt (and often grant creation) via the key policy, combined with an ECR repository policy permitting the cross-account pull, satisfying least privilege. KMS key material cannot be copied across accounts (D), and ECR fully supports customer-managed KMS encryption including cross-account access, contradicting C.

stem: A team runs a web application on an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer and wants zero-downtime deployments that automatically provision a full replacement fleet, shift traffic once the new fleet is healthy, and terminate the old fleet only after a bake period confirms stability. Which CodeDeploy deployment type should they configure?

choices.text: In-place deployment with CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce.

Blue/green deployment, in which CodeDeploy provisions a replacement Auto Scaling group, registers new instances with the load balancer only after health checks pass, reroutes traffic, and terminates the original instances after a configurable wait period.
In-place deployment with CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime, relying on rolling instance-by-instance updates on the existing fleet.
CodeDeploy does not support any replacement-fleet deployment for EC2/ASG, so this cannot be achieved.

explanation: CodeDeploy blue/green for EC2/ASG provisions a new replacement environment, validates instance health before shifting load balancer traffic, and terminates the original instances after a specified termination wait time, matching every requirement described. In-place deployments (A, C) update the existing fleet directly rather than provisioning a separate replacement environment.

stem: A team deploying an ECS service must choose between an ECS native rolling update and a CodeDeploy-managed blue/green deployment. They require shifting a small percentage of production traffic to the new task set, monitoring CloudWatch alarms, and automatically rolling back before most users are affected. Which approach meets this, and why is the alternative insufficient?

choices.text: ECS native rolling updates, because they always shift traffic gradually in small percentage increments with automatic alarm-based rollback.

CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS, because it supports canary and linear traffic-shifting configurations with CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback, whereas ECS's native rolling update replaces tasks based on desired count and health check grace period without weighted traffic shifting or alarm-triggered rollback.
Both approaches are functionally identical for traffic shifting and rollback.
Rolling updates are preferred because they support traffic-shifting percentages while blue/green does not.

explanation: Only CodeDeploy-managed ECS blue/green deployments provide configurable canary or linear traffic shifting between two task sets combined with CloudWatch alarm-triggered automatic rollback; ECS's native rolling update simply replaces tasks incrementally with no weighted traffic control. Option D reverses the actual capabilities of the two mechanisms.

stem: A team wants to shift 10% of production traffic to a new Lambda function version, monitor error rates for 10 minutes, and then automatically shift the remaining 90% if no CloudWatch alarm fires, using an alias for the production endpoint. Which CodeDeploy deployment configuration fits this?

choices.text: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce

A predefined canary configuration such as CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes, which shifts 10% of traffic, waits 10 minutes while monitoring associated alarms, then shifts the remaining 90% if rollback was not triggered.
A linear configuration that shifts traffic in equal increments every minute until reaching 100%.
Lambda does not support traffic shifting between versions; only full cutover is supported.

explanation: CodeDeploy provides predefined Lambda canary configurations, such as LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes, matching an initial percentage, a bake period, then a full shift via the routed alias. LambdaAllAtOnce (A) shifts 100% immediately with no canary phase, and Lambda does support alias-based traffic shifting, making D false.

stem: A team running workloads on Amazon EKS wants to implement blue/green and canary deployment strategies similar to what CodeDeploy provides natively for ECS and Lambda, but CodeDeploy does not natively manage EKS deployments. What is an appropriate way to implement these strategies within their CI/CD pipeline?

choices.text: Use CodeDeploy's ECS blue/green deployment type, since it also directly manages EKS deployments.

Use a Kubernetes-native progressive delivery tool such as Argo Rollouts or Flagger, invoked from a CodeBuild or CodePipeline stage, to manage canary/blue-green rollouts with traffic weighting and automated rollback based on metrics.
Manually edit Kubernetes Deployment replica counts to simulate blue/green deployments with no automation.
EKS deployments must always use a simple rolling update with no possibility of canary or blue/green patterns.

explanation: Because CodeDeploy does not natively manage EKS/Kubernetes deployments, progressive delivery tools like Argo Rollouts or Flagger are the standard way to implement canary/blue-green strategies on Kubernetes, orchestrated from a CodePipeline/CodeBuild stage. Option A is incorrect since CodeDeploy's ECS deployment type is specific to Amazon ECS, not EKS.

stem: A platform team is defining deployment standards and must explain the difference between mutable and immutable deployment patterns for EC2-based applications. Which statement correctly describes this distinction?

choices.text: Mutable deployments update code in place on existing running instances, risking configuration drift and partial-update states; immutable deployments provision entirely new instances with the new version and replace the old ones, avoiding in-place changes to running infrastructure.
Mutable deployments always use containers, while immutable deployments always use virtual machines.
Immutable deployments modify the existing instance's operating system without replacing any infrastructure, while mutable deployments always replace the entire fleet.
There is no practical difference; both terms describe the same deployment mechanism.

explanation: The mutable versus immutable distinction is exactly whether existing infrastructure is updated in place (mutable, e.g., CodeDeploy in-place) versus replaced wholesale with new infrastructure built from a new artifact or AMI (immutable, e.g., blue/green), which directly affects drift risk and rollback simplicity. Statement C reverses the correct definitions.

stem: A stateful application stores session data on an instance-attached EBS volume that is not shared or replicated, and the team is considering moving from CodeDeploy in-place deployments to blue/green to reduce deployment risk. What key tradeoff must they address first?

choices.text: Blue/green deployments automatically migrate EBS volume data to new instances at no additional configuration cost, so there is no tradeoff.

Because blue/green provisions entirely new instances with fresh EBS volumes, state stored only on the original instance's volume will not automatically carry over; the team must externalize session state to a shared store such as ElastiCache, DynamoDB, or EFS before adopting blue/green.
Blue/green deployments cannot be used with any application that uses EBS volumes under any circumstances.
In-place deployments also always lose local EBS data on every deployment, so there is no difference between the approaches.

explanation: Blue/green deployments create new instances with fresh EBS volumes, so instance-local state is not preserved automatically; applications with such local state should externalize it to a shared, durable store before adopting blue/green. In-place deployments (D) update the same instances and attached volumes, so they do not share this data-loss characteristic.

stem: A static website hosted in S3 and served through CloudFront needs a blue/green deployment approach so a new version can be fully validated before any production users see it, with an instant, low-risk cutover and easy rollback. Which architecture best supports this?

choices.text: Overwrite the objects in the existing S3 bucket directly with the new version, relying on CloudFront cache invalidation, with no separate validation environment.

Deploy the new version to a separate S3 bucket or origin, validate it independently, then cut production traffic over by updating the CloudFront distribution's origin configuration, keeping the old bucket intact for instant rollback.
Use CodeDeploy's ValidateService hook directly against the S3 bucket, since CodeDeploy manages S3 static website deployments in place.
Blue/green deployment concepts do not apply to static content served from S3/CloudFront.

explanation: Using a separate bucket or origin for the new version, validating it independently, and then updating the CloudFront origin configuration to cut over achieves a true blue/green pattern with instant rollback by simply reverting the origin change. Overwriting the same bucket (A) provides no isolated validation environment or clean rollback path.

stem: An application deployed via CodeDeploy blue/green to EC2 instances stores uploaded user files on an Amazon EFS file system mounted by all instances. When the new green fleet is provisioned, what is the correct expectation regarding this shared storage, and what should the team verify?

choices.text: EFS data will not be accessible until it is manually copied to the new fleet, since EBS and EFS behave identically in blue/green deployments.

Because EFS is a shared, network-attached file system rather than an instance-local volume, the green fleet can mount the same EFS file system as the blue fleet, so shared data remains accessible; the team should verify the launch configuration mounts the correct file system and that security groups and NFS ports allow access.
Blue/green deployments require a completely separate EFS file system for the green fleet, effectively duplicating all data.
EFS cannot be used with Auto Scaling groups under any circumstances.

explanation: Unlike instance-local EBS volumes, EFS is a shared network file system that any properly configured instance can mount concurrently, so shared application data naturally remains available to a new fleet as long as mount targets, security groups, and launch configuration are correct. Option A incorrectly equates EBS and EFS behavior, which differ significantly here.

stem: A team is choosing a CodeDeploy deployment configuration for an in-place EC2 deployment behind an ELB with 20 instances, wanting to balance deployment speed against the risk of taking too much capacity offline at once, without writing a custom configuration. How do the built-in extremes compare, and what fills the middle ground?

choices.text: CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce deploys to all instances simultaneously for maximum speed but removes all capacity at once; CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime deploys to a single instance at a time for minimum risk but the slowest overall deployment; a percentage-based custom configuration balances the two.
CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime always deploys to all 20 instances concurrently regardless of its name.
CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce is the safest option because it completes fastest, minimizing the deployment window.
Deployment configurations only apply to Lambda and ECS deployments, not EC2/in-place deployments.

explanation: AllAtOnce maximizes speed at the cost of taking all capacity offline simultaneously, while OneAtATime minimizes risk at the cost of speed, and a custom percentage-based configuration provides a middle ground between the two extremes. Deployment configurations fully apply to EC2/in-place deployments, making D false.

stem: A CodeDeploy deployment to an EC2 fleet fails partway through because a lifecycle hook script returns a non-zero exit code on several instances, but the deployment group has no automatic rollback configured and no CloudWatch alarms attached. What happens to the fleet after this failure?

choices.text: CodeDeploy automatically rolls back all instances to the previous version regardless of configuration, since rollback is always enabled by default.

The deployment stops and is marked Failed; instances that already succeeded remain on the new version while the failed instances are left inconsistent, and manual intervention such as redeploying the previous revision is required to restore consistency.
CodeDeploy automatically terminates all instances in the fleet after any lifecycle hook failure.
The failure is ignored, and CodeDeploy marks the deployment as Succeeded despite the hook failures.

explanation: Without automatic rollback configured (on failure or on alarm), a failed CodeDeploy deployment simply stops in a partially-updated state; restoring consistency requires manually redeploying the last known-good revision or enabling rollback beforehand. CodeDeploy does not roll back by default (A is false), nor does it terminate instances or silently report success (C, D false).

stem: A team is adopting blue/green deployments for an application backed by a single shared RDS database, where the new application version requires a backward-incompatible schema change. What is the primary challenge, and what is the recommended mitigation?

choices.text: There is no challenge, because blue/green deployments always provision an independent, automatically migrated copy of the database.

Both the old and new application versions may run simultaneously against the same shared database during the traffic-shifting window, so a breaking schema change can fail the old version still receiving traffic; the recommended mitigation is expand-and-contract migration, deploying additive changes first and removing deprecated columns only in a later release.
The database should be deleted and recreated during every blue/green deployment to avoid this issue.
This challenge only applies to Lambda deployments, not to EC2 or ECS blue/green deployments sharing an RDS instance.

explanation: When compute is deployed blue/green but the database is shared, both versions can run concurrently during cutover, so schema changes must remain backward compatible via an expand-and-contract pattern to avoid breaking the still-active old version. This challenge applies broadly to any blue/green compute deployment sharing one database, not just Lambda, making D incorrect.

stem: A team must choose between a linear and a canary traffic-shifting configuration for a Lambda deployment using CodeDeploy and wants to understand the fundamental difference between the two shifting patterns. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Canary shifts traffic in a single initial increment, then waits a specified time before shifting the remainder all at once, while linear shifts traffic in equal, repeating increments at a fixed interval until reaching 100%.
Linear and canary are two names for the exact same behavior in CodeDeploy.
Canary always completes the traffic shift in exactly two steps of 50% each.
Linear deployments require manual approval between each traffic increment, while canary deployments do not.

explanation: CodeDeploy's canary configuration shifts a defined percentage once and waits before shifting the remainder to 100%, whereas linear configurations shift traffic in equal steps repeated at a fixed interval until fully shifted, a clear structural difference. Canary percentages are not fixed at 50/50 (C is false), and neither pattern requires manual approval by default (D is false).

stem: A CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for an ECS service repeatedly fails because the new task set is marked unhealthy and rolled back before the application finishes a lengthy startup process involving loading large in-memory caches, even though it eventually becomes healthy about 3 minutes after starting. What change is most likely to resolve this?

choices.text: Increase the health check grace period and tune the target group's health check thresholds and interval so the warm-up process has time to complete before being marked unhealthy.
Reduce the number of tasks in the new task set to speed up startup.
Switch from blue/green to an in-place ECS rolling update, which has no health check requirements.
Disable health checks entirely on the target group so CodeDeploy cannot mark the deployment as failed.

explanation: Extending the health check grace period and tuning target group health check settings gives a slow-starting application enough time to become healthy before being marked failed, directly addressing the warm-up delay. Disabling health checks (D) removes the safety mechanism entirely, and rolling updates (C) still depend on service health/stability, so they do not avoid the underlying issue.

stem: Which statement correctly describes how AWS SAM templates are processed when deployed?

choices.text: SAM CLI compiles the template into a Terraform configuration before applying it via Terraform Cloud.
The AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 transform macro expands SAM's simplified syntax, such as AWS::Serverless::Function, into standard CloudFormation resources during deployment.
SAM templates are deployed directly by the Lambda service without ever going through CloudFormation.
SAM requires a separate SAM Registry account to convert templates before they can be uploaded to CloudFormation.

explanation: The Transform section invokes the Serverless Application Model macro, which CloudFormation expands server-side into full resource definitions (Lambda functions, IAM roles, API Gateway resources) before creating a change set. SAM stacks are still ordinary CloudFormation stacks; Lambda and Terraform play no role in this expansion.

stem: A team currently maintains large, repetitive CloudFormation JSON templates for dozens of similar microservice stacks and wants to reduce duplication using loops, conditionals, and typed objects while still being able to inspect the exact resources that will be created before deployment. Which approach best satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Rewrite the templates using CloudFormation macros exclusively, since macros are the only way to add programming logic to CloudFormation.
Adopt the AWS CDK, define reusable constructs in a general-purpose language, and use cdk synth to render and review the resulting CloudFormation templates before cdk deploy.
Migrate to AWS OpsWorks stacks, which natively support loops and conditionals in Chef recipes.
