Use nested stacks exclusively, since nested stacks eliminate the need for repeated resource declarations.

explanation: CDK lets teams write infrastructure in a general-purpose language with loops, conditionals, and reusable constructs, and cdk synth produces the literal CloudFormation template for review before deployment, satisfying both requirements. Macros can add logic but don't provide typed objects or a full programming language, and OpsWorks or plain nested stacks don't address templating duplication the same way.

stem: An engineer discovers that a production CloudFormation stack shows several resources as MODIFIED after running drift detection, including a security group whose inbound rules were changed manually during an incident. The team wants to reconcile the stack to match the current, drifted production configuration without immediately reverting the manual change, while still being able to manage the resource with CloudFormation going forward. What should they do?

choices.text: Delete and recreate the stack from the original template so CloudFormation re-provisions all resources with their original configuration.
Update the CloudFormation template to reflect the drifted security group rules, then run a change set and review it to confirm no unintended changes before executing the update.
Run aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback to force the stack to accept the current resource state as the new baseline.
Ignore the drift result since CloudFormation automatically reconciles drifted resources during the next stack update.

explanation: To reconcile an intentional out-of-band change, the template must be updated to match the drifted state, and a change set lets the team preview that the update will not inadvertently revert or break other resources before applying it. CloudFormation does not auto-heal drift, and continue-update-rollback addresses failed rollbacks, not drift reconciliation.

stem: A cloud platform team wants to publish a governed, versioned building block that provisions a standardized VPC, with specific subnet counts, NACLs, and flow log configuration, so that other teams can embed it directly inside their own CloudFormation templates as a single resource type, with updates rolled out by publishing a new version. Which CloudFormation feature is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: AWS CloudFormation StackSets
A CloudFormation module registered in the CloudFormation registry
A nested stack referenced via a hardcoded S3 URL
An AWS Service Catalog product with a launch constraint

explanation: CloudFormation modules package a set of resources as a reusable, versioned schema that other templates consume as a native resource type, fitting the requirement to embed the block as a resource with versioned rollout precisely. StackSets deploy whole stacks across accounts or regions rather than being embedded as a resource, and Service Catalog governs self-service product provisioning rather than in-template composition.

stem: A mobile backend team wants to roll out a new pricing algorithm to a Lambda-based API gradually, monitor CloudWatch alarms during the rollout, and automatically halt and roll back the configuration change if error rates spike, without redeploying application code. Which AWS service is designed for this use case?

choices.text: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with standard parameters
AWS AppConfig with a deployment strategy that defines gradual rollout percentage and time, plus a CloudWatch alarm configured as a monitor
AWS CloudFormation change sets with manual approval
AWS Secrets Manager automatic rotation

explanation: AppConfig is purpose-built for dynamic configuration and feature flag rollout, supporting deployment strategies with bake time and percentage-based rollout, and it can automatically roll back a deployment when an associated CloudWatch alarm triggers. Parameter Store lacks built-in gradual rollout and automatic rollback monitoring.

stem: A DevOps team is deciding where to store two categories of configuration data used by their CI/CD pipeline: database credentials that must rotate automatically every 30 days, and non-sensitive environment names and feature toggles referenced by dozens of CloudFormation templates. Which approach is most cost-effective and appropriate?

choices.text: Store both categories in AWS Secrets Manager, since it is the only service that integrates with CloudFormation dynamic references.
Store the database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled, and store the non-sensitive configuration values in Systems Manager Parameter Store standard parameters.
Store both categories in Systems Manager Parameter Store advanced parameters with a custom Lambda rotation schedule.
Store the database credentials in Parameter Store SecureString parameters with a manually scheduled Lambda rotation function, and store the toggles in Secrets Manager.

explanation: Secrets Manager provides native automatic rotation for credentials like database passwords, while Parameter Store standard parameters are free and well suited for non-sensitive configuration values referenced across many templates; both support CloudFormation dynamic references. Storing everything in Secrets Manager incurs unnecessary cost and complexity for values that are not secrets.

stem: A legacy application managed with AWS OpsWorks Stacks uses Chef recipes to configure application servers. An operator needs to run a recipe that installs a new monitoring agent every time a new instance is added to a layer, before the instance starts serving traffic. Which OpsWorks lifecycle event should this recipe be assigned to?

choices.text: Deploy
Setup
Configure
Shutdown

explanation: The Setup lifecycle event runs once, right after an instance boots and before it starts accepting traffic, making it the correct place for one-time agent installation on new instances. Configure runs on all stack instances whenever the stack's configuration changes, such as another instance joining, and Deploy only applies when an application is deployed.

stem: A team is deciding between CloudFormation nested stacks and cross-stack references, using Export and Fn::ImportValue, to share a VPC's subnet IDs with multiple independently owned application stacks. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two approaches?

choices.text: Cross-stack references let the VPC stack be updated or deleted freely at any time even while other stacks import its outputs, whereas nested stacks always block updates to the parent.

Nested stacks tie the child stack's lifecycle to the parent and are best when one team owns the whole hierarchy, while cross-stack exports allow independently owned stacks to consume shared values but CloudFormation blocks changing or deleting an exported output while any import of it still exists.
Cross-stack references require the AWS::CloudFormation::Stack resource type, while nested stacks use Fn::ImportValue.
Nested stacks and cross-stack references are functionally identical; the only difference is template file organization.

explanation: Nested stacks are appropriate when a single owner manages a tightly coupled hierarchy of resources, since child stacks are updated and deleted together with the parent, whereas exported outputs consumed via Fn::ImportValue support decoupled ownership across stacks, though CloudFormation prevents changing or deleting an exported output while it is still imported elsewhere. The other options invert or misstate these mechanics.

stem: A team deploys a CloudFormation stack set to 25 target accounts across 3 regions. During a recent update, several stack instances failed simultaneously and the operation stopped after failures exceeded the configured threshold, leaving many accounts un-updated. What is the most likely explanation, and what should the team change to complete rollouts more reliably in the future?

choices.text: StackSets does not support failure tolerance settings; the team must manually retry every failed account, and there is no way to change this behavior.

The stack set operation preferences had a low FailureToleranceCount and a low MaxConcurrentCount that caused the operation to halt early; increasing the failure tolerance and fixing the root cause template or permissions error allows subsequent operations to proceed further before stopping.
StackSets always halts entirely after any single failure regardless of configuration, so the only fix is to split the stack set into 25 separate individual stacks.
The failures indicate that StackSets requires all target accounts to be in the same OU, and the team must remove accounts from other OUs.

explanation: Stack set operation preferences, including FailureToleranceCount or Percentage and MaxConcurrentCount or Percentage, control how many failures are tolerated before an operation stops, so tuning these settings alongside fixing the underlying template or permissions issue lets deployments proceed further. StackSets does support configurable failure tolerance, contradicting the claim that no control exists, and OU membership is not the constraint described here.

stem: A security engineer wants to enforce, at synthesis time, that every S3 bucket defined anywhere in a large multi-stack AWS CDK application has server-side encryption enabled, and wants CDK synthesis to fail with a clear error if a developer forgets to configure it. Which CDK mechanism is designed for this kind of cross-cutting validation?

choices.text: A CloudFormation StackSet applied after deployment to detect unencrypted buckets
A CDK Aspect that visits every construct in the construct tree during synthesis and adds a validation error if an S3 bucket lacks encryption
An AWS Config rule that flags non-compliant buckets after they are created
A CDK context value set in cdk.json that automatically enables encryption on all buckets

explanation: Aspects implement a visitor pattern that CDK applies across the entire construct tree during synthesis, making them the standard mechanism for cross-cutting checks like enforcing encryption and failing the build via Annotations.addError. Config rules and post-deployment detection only catch violations after resources already exist, not at synthesis time.

stem: A CloudFormation stack uses a custom resource backed by a Lambda function to look up an AMI ID from a third-party API during stack creation. The stack creation hangs for over an hour and eventually times out with Custom Resource failed to stabilize in expected time. Lambda logs show the function executed successfully and returned a response. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The custom resource's Lambda function returned its response directly instead of sending a properly formatted SUCCESS or FAILED signal to the pre-signed S3 response URL provided in the event.
CloudFormation custom resources cannot invoke Lambda functions that call external HTTP APIs.
The stack's IAM role lacks permission to invoke Lambda functions.
The custom resource must be replaced with a CloudFormation macro, since custom resources do not support asynchronous operations.

explanation: A custom resource's backing Lambda function must explicitly send a response payload, including Status and PhysicalResourceId, to the pre-signed S3 URL supplied in the event; if it merely returns a value instead of sending that signal, CloudFormation never receives confirmation and eventually times out, even though the function itself ran successfully. The other options misdiagnose IAM permissions or an architectural limitation that don't match the symptoms described.

stem: An enterprise onboarding team wants every new AWS account created for business units to automatically receive a standardized VPC, mandatory guardrails, centralized logging to a log archive account, and enrollment in AWS Config and CloudTrail, without engineers manually configuring each new account. Which AWS Control Tower capability directly automates this account creation and baseline setup?

choices.text: AWS Control Tower Account Factory
AWS Organizations service control policies alone
AWS Config conformance packs alone
AWS Service Catalog without Control Tower integration

explanation: Account Factory automates provisioning of new accounts with a pre-approved baseline, including networking, guardrails, and centralized logging, CloudTrail, and Config setup, directly addressing this requirement. SCPs and conformance packs enforce policy but do not provision the account and its baseline resources themselves.

stem: A team enables an AWS Control Tower guardrail that prevents member accounts from disabling AWS Config in the region where Control Tower operates, and a separate guardrail that reports when S3 buckets are publicly accessible. How would these two guardrails be classified, respectively?

choices.text: Both are preventive guardrails implemented as SCPs.
The first is a preventive guardrail implemented via SCP, and the second is a detective guardrail implemented via an AWS Config rule that reports non-compliance rather than blocking the action.
The first is detective, and the second is preventive, because S3 bucket policies are enforced at creation time.
Both are detective guardrails, since Control Tower guardrails never block API calls.

explanation: Preventive guardrails are implemented using SCPs and block prohibited actions outright, such as disabling Config, while detective guardrails use AWS Config rules to identify non-compliant resources after the fact, such as flagging public S3 buckets. This matches the standard Control Tower guardrail taxonomy; the other options mismatch the mechanisms.

stem: A third-party monitoring vendor needs to assume a role in a customer's AWS account to collect metrics. The customer creates an IAM role with a trust policy allowing the vendor's AWS account to assume it, but during testing, the vendor's AssumeRole calls fail with Access denied. The vendor confirms they are passing an ExternalId value in their AssumeRole call. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: AssumeRole calls can never include an ExternalId parameter when the trusted principal is a different AWS account.

The role's trust policy does not include a Condition block requiring sts:ExternalId to match the value the customer assigned to the vendor, or the value the vendor provided does not match what is configured in the trust policy.
Cross-account role assumption is only possible if both accounts belong to the same AWS Organizations organization.
The vendor must use IAM Identity Center instead of AssumeRole for any cross-account access.

explanation: When protecting against the confused deputy problem with a third party, the trust policy must include a Condition requiring sts:ExternalId to equal an agreed-upon value; if that condition is missing or the values don't match exactly, AssumeRole fails with access denied even though the trusted principal is correct. ExternalId is explicitly supported for external-account trust relationships, and cross-account role assumption works without both accounts being in the same Organization.

stem: An account sits in an OU nested three levels deep under the Organizations root: Root, then Security-OU, then Prod-OU, then Payments-OU. The Root has an SCP denying ec2:TerminateInstances for all accounts. The Prod-OU has an SCP explicitly allowing ec2:TerminateInstances. Engineers in the account report they still cannot terminate EC2 instances. What explains this behavior?

choices.text: SCPs at lower-level OUs always override SCPs at higher-level OUs, so the Prod-OU allow statement should have taken effect; this must be an AWS service issue.
SCPs are allow lists only by default at the root, and an explicit Allow at any level always overrides a Deny at another level.

SCPs from every level in the hierarchy are evaluated together, and an explicit Deny at any level blocks the action account-wide; an Allow statement elsewhere cannot override a Deny from an ancestor OU.
The account must also have an identity-based policy explicitly denying the action for the Root SCP to take effect.

explanation: SCPs are cumulative down the OU hierarchy: the effective permissions for an account are the intersection of all SCPs from the root down to the account, and an explicit Deny at any level always wins over an Allow elsewhere in the hierarchy, so the Root-level deny still blocks termination despite the Prod-OU allow. SCPs never grant permissions by themselves; they only filter what IAM policies can otherwise allow, and an Allow statement cannot override an ancestor's explicit Deny.

stem: A company wants a centralized security team to manage GuardDuty configuration and view findings for all 120 accounts in their AWS Organization, while avoiding the operational burden of manually enabling GuardDuty in every account as new accounts are created. Which approach should they use?

choices.text: Designate a delegated administrator account for GuardDuty and enable auto-enable for new organization accounts, so GuardDuty automatically activates and reports findings to the delegated administrator as accounts join.
Ask each of the 120 account owners to individually enable GuardDuty and manually invite the security team's account as a GuardDuty member.
Use AWS Config rules to enforce that GuardDuty is enabled, since Config rules can automatically activate GuardDuty in non-compliant accounts.
Enable GuardDuty only in the AWS Organizations management account, since it automatically monitors all member accounts by default.

explanation: GuardDuty's Organizations integration lets a delegated administrator account centrally manage all member accounts and enable auto-enable so new accounts are automatically protected without manual invitations. Config rules can flag non-compliance but cannot activate GuardDuty themselves, and GuardDuty does not automatically monitor all accounts just because it is enabled in the management account.

stem: A platform team wants developers to be able to request new isolated sandbox AWS accounts through a self-service catalog, with each request automatically triggering Control Tower's account provisioning workflow and applying the organization's standard guardrails, while restricting who can request accounts to members of an approved IAM group. Which combination achieves this?

choices.text: Provide direct AWS Organizations CreateAccount API access to all developers.

Publish the Control Tower Account Factory as an AWS Service Catalog product, share the associated portfolio only with the approved IAM group, and let Service Catalog handle provisioning through Control Tower's account vending workflow.
Have developers submit a support ticket to manually create accounts through the Control Tower console.
Use AWS Config conformance packs to automatically create new accounts when non-compliant resources are detected.

explanation: Control Tower's Account Factory is exposed as a Service Catalog product, so sharing its portfolio only with an approved group lets those developers self-service request accounts while Control Tower applies the guardrail baseline automatically; direct Organizations API access would bypass governance entirely. Config conformance packs are unrelated to account creation.

stem: A company wants to ensure that an S3 bucket used for centralized log storage can only be accessed by IAM principals belonging to their own AWS Organization, even if the bucket policy is later misconfigured to allow a broader principal, and wants this enforced consistently for every resource-based policy across the organization rather than editing each policy individually. Which control best achieves this?

choices.text: Add aws:PrincipalOrgID as a condition to the S3 bucket policy only, since this is sufficient for organization-wide enforcement.

Create a Service Control Policy with a Deny statement for relevant actions when the condition aws:PrincipalOrgID does not equal the organization's ID, applied at the root, so every resource-based policy across all accounts is effectively constrained without editing each one.
Use AWS Config to detect and delete overly permissive bucket policies after they are created.
Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level, which restricts access to only organization members.

explanation: An SCP using the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key applied at the root level acts as an organization-wide guardrail that blocks access from principals outside the organization regardless of how individual resource policies are written, achieving consistent enforcement without editing every policy. Relying on the bucket policy alone does not protect against future misconfiguration, and Block Public Access only prevents public access, not access from principals outside the org.

stem: An account governed by AWS Control Tower shows a drifted status in the Control Tower console after an administrator manually modified the account's baseline CloudTrail configuration outside of Control Tower. What is the recommended way to resolve this drift?

choices.text: Delete and re-register the account with AWS Organizations to force Control Tower to reset it.
Manually revert the CloudTrail change and take no further action, since Control Tower automatically clears the drifted status on its own schedule.
Re-register or repair the affected OU or account in the Control Tower console, or update the landing zone, which re-applies the baseline and guardrails to bring the account back into compliance.
Attach an SCP that blocks all CloudTrail API calls in that account permanently to prevent any future changes.

explanation: Control Tower provides a mechanism to detect drift and remediate it by re-registering or repairing the account or OU, or updating the landing zone, which reapplies the baseline configuration including CloudTrail settings. Simply reverting manually does not reliably clear the drifted status Control Tower tracks, and deleting and re-adding the account or blanket-denying CloudTrail are disruptive and not the standard remediation path.

stem: A finance team requires that every EC2 instance and S3 bucket created across all accounts in the organization carry a CostCenter tag with a value from an approved list, and wants non-compliant tagging to be flagged for correction rather than blocking resource creation outright. Which AWS Organizations feature should they use, and how does it behave?

choices.text: A Service Control Policy that denies resource creation unless the CostCenter tag is present, since SCPs are the only way to enforce tagging.

A tag policy defined in AWS Organizations that specifies allowed values for the CostCenter tag key; tag policies report noncompliant tagging in compliance reports but do not by themselves block resource creation.
AWS Budgets, which can automatically enforce mandatory tags on all new resources.
AWS Config rules only, since AWS Organizations has no tagging enforcement feature.

explanation: AWS Organizations tag policies let you define standardized tag keys and allowed values across accounts, and non-compliant resources are reported through the tag policy compliance report rather than being blocked at creation time, matching the requirement to flag rather than block. An SCP could enforce a hard block but that contradicts the stated requirement, and Budgets does not enforce tagging.

stem: An automation pipeline running in Account A assumes a cross-account role in Account B to run a long CloudFormation deployment that regularly takes 90 minutes. The pipeline fails partway through with The security token included in the request is expired. The role's trust policy is correctly configured, and the pipeline uses AssumeRole once at the start. What is the most likely fix?

choices.text: Increase the role's MaxSessionDuration setting, up to 12 hours, and request a longer DurationSeconds in the AssumeRole call, since the default maximum session length for an assumed role is only 1 hour unless MaxSessionDuration is explicitly configured higher.
Switch from AssumeRole to GetFederationToken, which never expires.
The pipeline must call AssumeRole again every 15 minutes regardless of any session duration setting, since STS tokens cannot be configured for longer than 15 minutes.
Add the sts:ExternalId condition to the trust policy, which extends session duration automatically.

explanation: By default, assumed-role sessions are limited to a maximum of 1 hour unless the role's MaxSessionDuration attribute is increased, up to 12 hours, and the caller requests a matching DurationSeconds, which would let the 90-minute pipeline run without the credentials expiring mid-deployment. GetFederationToken credentials also expire and are unrelated to role assumption, and ExternalId is a security condition unrelated to session length.

stem: A security team wants an automated remediation workflow: when a specific AWS Config rule reports a non-compliant security group, the workflow should first notify the resource owner via SNS, wait up to 4 hours for manual approval via a callback, and if not approved in time, automatically revoke the offending inbound rule using a Lambda function, logging every step for audit purposes. Which architecture best supports this?

choices.text: A single Lambda function that sleeps for 4 hours before revoking the rule.

An AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow using a Task state with a callback pattern (waitForTaskToken) for the approval step, a Choice state to branch on approval or timeout, and a Task state invoking Lambda to revoke the rule, with execution history providing the audit trail.
An AWS Step Functions Express Workflow, since Express workflows are optimized for long-running human-approval steps lasting hours.
An EventBridge rule that directly invokes the remediation Lambda function without any orchestration, relying on Lambda's own retry policy for the approval wait.

explanation: Step Functions Standard Workflows support executions up to one year and the waitForTaskToken callback pattern, which is designed for pausing until an external approval or timeout occurs, with built-in execution history for auditing. A Lambda function sleeping for hours would waste function duration and risk timeouts, and Express Workflows are optimized for short-duration, high-volume workloads up to 5 minutes, not multi-hour waits.

stem: A team wants any S3 bucket found by an AWS Config rule to have public read access automatically remediated within minutes by removing the offending bucket policy statement, without requiring a human to review every finding. Which AWS Config feature should be configured alongside the rule?

choices.text: A Config aggregator, which can automatically remediate non-compliant resources across accounts.
A remediation configuration attached to the Config rule that specifies an SSM Automation document to run automatically upon a NON_COMPLIANT evaluation.
A CloudWatch alarm on the Config rule's compliance metric that pages an on-call engineer.
AWS Trusted Advisor, which automatically fixes any Config rule violation it detects.

explanation: AWS Config supports attaching an automatic remediation action, typically a Systems Manager Automation document, to a rule so that a NON_COMPLIANT evaluation triggers remediation without human intervention, directly meeting the requirement for automatic remediation within minutes. Aggregators only aggregate compliance data, and Trusted Advisor does not perform remediation for Config rule violations.

stem: A team needs an AWS Config rule enforcing organization-specific logic: any DynamoDB table tagged Classification=Restricted must have point-in-time recovery enabled, while tables without that tag are exempt. No AWS managed Config rule expresses this conditional relationship between a tag value and a resource setting. How should they implement the check?

choices.text: Use the managed rule required-tags only, since it can natively express arbitrary conditional relationships between a tag value and another resource property.

Create a custom Config rule backed by an AWS Lambda function that receives the configuration item, evaluates the custom classification logic, and returns a compliance status to Config via the PutEvaluations API.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor custom checks, since Trusted Advisor is designed for organization-specific compliance logic.
Write the check as a CloudFormation Hook, since Config does not support any form of custom evaluation logic.

explanation: When required logic goes beyond simple tag presence checks, AWS Config allows custom rules backed by a Lambda function that evaluates resources against custom logic and reports results back to Config via PutEvaluations, which fits this exact scenario. The managed required-tags rule can verify tag key and value presence but cannot express a conditional relationship tying a tag value to another resource setting, and Trusted Advisor and CloudFormation Hooks are not designed for this kind of Config compliance evaluation.

stem: An engineer needs to immediately restart a specific service on 10 EC2 instances right now, as a one-off ad hoc action, without building a reusable multi-step workflow. Which Systems Manager capability is the simplest fit?

choices.text: Systems Manager Automation with a custom runbook
Systems Manager Run Command, targeting the instances by tag or instance ID and executing the built-in AWS-RunShellScript document
Systems Manager State Manager association
Systems Manager Distributor

explanation: Run Command is designed for simple, immediate, ad hoc command execution across one or more managed instances without needing to author a multi-step Automation runbook. Automation and State Manager are better suited to multi-step orchestration or continuously enforced desired state, which is unnecessary overhead for a single one-off restart.

stem: A team is building two separate automation workflows: a high-volume IoT telemetry transformation pipeline processing millions of short-lived events per day, each completing in under a second, and a compliance remediation workflow that occasionally runs for several hours and must be individually auditable with exactly-once execution semantics and a full retained execution history. Which Step Functions workflow types should they choose, respectively?

choices.text: Standard for both, since Standard Workflows are always the correct default choice.

Express Workflow for the high-volume short-duration pipeline, since it is optimized for high event rates at lower cost with durations up to 5 minutes, and Standard Workflow for the remediation process, since it provides exactly-once execution and supports long durations with durable execution history.
Standard for the telemetry pipeline because it is high-volume, and Express for the remediation workflow because it is infrequent.
Express for both, since Express Workflows support the same durable execution history as Standard Workflows by default.

explanation: Express Workflows are designed for high-volume, short-duration event processing at lower cost with at-least-once semantics, while Standard Workflows provide exactly-once execution, support durations up to a year, and retain full execution history for auditing, matching the remediation workflow's requirements. Reversing the choices or defaulting to one type for both ignores the cost and durability tradeoffs each type is optimized for.

stem: A custom automation script using the AWS SDK to call the CloudFormation and EC2 APIs across dozens of accounts intermittently fails with Rate exceeded ThrottlingException errors, particularly during large parallel batch operations. The team wants to make the script more resilient without simply reducing functionality. What should they implement?

choices.text: Catch the exception and immediately terminate the script, logging the failure for manual retry.

Configure the SDK client to use exponential backoff with jitter for retries, which many AWS SDKs support natively via retry configuration, and reduce the number of concurrent API calls or use adaptive retry mode where available.
Switch from the SDK to the AWS CLI, which is immune to API throttling.
Request an increase to the Lambda concurrency limit, since throttling is always caused by Lambda concurrency settings.

explanation: AWS SDKs provide configurable retry strategies, including exponential backoff with jitter and adaptive retry modes, which are the standard resilience pattern for handling transient throttling from AWS service API rate limits; reducing concurrency further mitigates the underlying rate pressure. The CLI is subject to the same service-side API rate limits as the SDK, and Lambda concurrency is unrelated unless the script itself runs in Lambda and is throttled by its own concurrency, which is not indicated here.

stem: A compliance team needs to continuously verify that all managed EC2 instances are running an approved version of a specific security agent, and generate a report of instances that are out of compliance for auditing. Which combination of services provides this capability with minimal custom development?

choices.text: Systems Manager Inventory to collect installed application and version data from managed instances, combined with an AWS Config custom rule that flags instances without the approved agent version as non-compliant.
AWS Trusted Advisor, which natively reports on installed software versions across all EC2 instances.
Amazon Inspector network reachability rules, which report on installed agent versions.
AWS CloudTrail log analysis using Athena queries against API call history.

explanation: Systems Manager Inventory collects detailed metadata about installed applications on managed instances, and this data can be evaluated against a Config custom rule to continuously flag non-compliant instances for reporting, requiring minimal custom coding beyond the evaluation logic. Trusted Advisor and Inspector network reachability rules do not report on arbitrary installed agent versions, and CloudTrail records API activity, not installed software inventory.

stem: A team wants a fully automated pipeline: whenever a specific security-relevant API call, such as opening port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 via ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, occurs anywhere in the account, the system should automatically evaluate the change, notify a Slack channel, and revoke the rule if it matches a disallowed pattern, all within seconds of the event, with clear visibility into each execution's steps for troubleshooting later. Which architecture is most appropriate?

choices.text: An AWS Config rule evaluated on the default periodic schedule of every 24 hours, which is fast enough for near real-time response.
A CloudTrail-based scheduled batch job running once per hour via a cron-triggered Lambda function that scans recent CloudTrail logs for the API call.

An Amazon EventBridge rule matching the CloudTrail-recorded API call in near real time, invoking an AWS Step Functions state machine that evaluates the change, posts to Slack, and conditionally invokes a Lambda function to revoke the rule, with Step Functions execution history providing per-step visibility.
An AWS Config custom rule triggered only on a configuration change, without any orchestration service, directly performing the Slack notification and remediation inside the rule's Lambda function.

explanation: EventBridge can match specific API calls captured by CloudTrail in near real time and trigger a Step Functions state machine, which provides clear per-step execution visibility while orchestrating evaluation, notification, and conditional remediation logic. Config's periodic or configuration-change-triggered rules and hourly batch scans are far slower than the within-seconds requirement, and performing everything inside a single Lambda function invoked by a Config rule sacrifices the step-by-step visibility requested.

stem: An operations team creates a State Manager association targeting 2,000 managed instances to apply a configuration update immediately. They want to avoid overwhelming instances or downstream systems by applying the change to all 2,000 instances simultaneously. Which State Manager association setting should they configure?

choices.text: MaxErrors only, since it is the only rate-related setting State Manager supports.

Rate control settings for the association, specifically MaxConcurrency to limit how many targets are processed simultaneously and MaxErrors to limit how many failures are tolerated before stopping, both configurable as counts or percentages.
A CloudWatch alarm that pauses the association automatically once a CPU threshold is breached across the fleet.
Systems Manager Maintenance Windows, since State Manager associations cannot control concurrency and must always run against a single instance at a time.

explanation: State Manager associations support rate control via MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors, letting operators throttle how many targets are updated in parallel and how many failures are tolerated, directly addressing the concern about overwhelming the fleet. MaxErrors alone does not control concurrency, and associations do support targeting many instances concurrently, contradicting the claim that they must run against a single instance at a time.

stem: A team currently manages a fleet of legacy application servers using AWS OpsWorks Stacks with custom Chef cookbooks for configuration management. They are evaluating whether to continue investing in OpsWorks-based automation or migrate configuration management responsibilities to AWS Systems Manager, using State Manager, Run Command, and Automation. Which consideration should most influence this decision?

choices.text: OpsWorks Stacks is the current recommended default for all new AWS configuration management workloads, so no migration should be considered.

Systems Manager integrates natively with AWS Config, Automation runbooks, and Parameter Store, and does not require operating a Chef or Puppet server, making it generally preferable for new automation investment, while existing OpsWorks workloads should be evaluated for migration given OpsWorks Stacks' comparatively lighter ongoing feature investment.
Chef and Puppet cookbooks written for OpsWorks Stacks can be executed natively without modification by Systems Manager Automation, so there is no meaningful difference between the two.
Systems Manager cannot manage on-premises or hybrid servers, so any workload with non-EC2 instances must remain on OpsWorks Stacks.

explanation: AWS has continued to invest heavily in Systems Manager's automation capabilities with tight integration into Config, EventBridge, and Parameter Store, and it does not require operating a Chef or Puppet server, which is a meaningful long-term operational tradeoff versus OpsWorks Stacks. Systems Manager does support hybrid and on-premises managed instances via the SSM Agent, contradicting the claim that it cannot, and Chef cookbooks are not natively portable to Systems Manager Automation without rework.

stem: A Step Functions state machine automates a multi-account resource cleanup task. One Task state invokes a Lambda function that occasionally fails due to a downstream API's transient throttling, causing the entire execution to fail immediately without retrying. The team wants the state machine to automatically retry that specific step a few times with exponential backoff before giving up and routing to a cleanup and notification path if all retries are exhausted. What should they add to the state machine definition?

choices.text: A Parallel state wrapping the Task, since Parallel states automatically retry failed branches.

A Retry field on the Task state specifying the error type or types to retry, along with IntervalSeconds, MaxAttempts, and BackoffRate, combined with a Catch field routing to the cleanup and notification state if retries are exhausted.
A Wait state placed before the Task state to always pause before execution, which prevents any throttling from ever occurring.
Nothing needs to change, since Step Functions automatically retries every Task state up to 3 times with no configuration required.

explanation: Step Functions supports per-state Retry configuration, specifying error types, interval, max attempts, and backoff rate, to automatically retry transient failures, and a Catch field can route to a fallback state once retries are exhausted, which is exactly the resilience pattern needed here. Step Functions does not automatically retry every Task state without explicit configuration, and a Parallel state or a blanket Wait state does not provide targeted retry and catch behavior for a specific transient error.

stem: A central automation team wants to run the same Systems Manager Automation runbook, for example to enforce a tagging standard, against target resources spread across 30 member accounts and 4 regions, initiating and monitoring all executions from a single management account, without logging into each target account individually. Which Systems Manager capability enables this?

choices.text: Systems Manager Run Command only, since Automation does not support any cross-account functionality.

Systems Manager Automation's cross-account, cross-region capability, which uses AWS Organizations integration and a designated administrator or delegated administrator account, along with an appropriately configured automation execution role in each target account, to run and track the runbook centrally.
Manually copying the Automation document to each of the 30 accounts and running it locally in each account's console.
AWS Config aggregators, which can directly execute Automation runbooks in aggregated accounts.

explanation: Systems Manager Automation supports cross-account, cross-region execution when integrated with AWS Organizations, allowing a designated account to centrally launch and monitor runbook executions across many target accounts and regions using per-account execution roles. Run Command lacks Automation's cross-account orchestration capability, and Config aggregators only aggregate compliance data; they cannot execute Automation runbooks.

stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance behind a fleet of application servers. During a recent AZ outage, RDS automatically failed over to the standby, but the application servers continued trying to connect to the old primary's IP address for several minutes, causing an extended outage. What is the MOST likely root cause, and how should the DevOps engineer fix it?

choices.text: The application caches the resolved IP address of the RDS endpoint's DNS CNAME beyond its TTL; the fix is to ensure the application respects the low TTL and re-resolves the DNS endpoint rather than caching the IP indefinitely.
RDS Multi-AZ does not update DNS records on failover; the fix is to implement a Lambda function that manually updates a Route 53 record after failover.
The DB instance is not using Aurora, and only Aurora supports automatic DNS failover; migrate to Aurora Multi-AZ.
Security group rules blocked traffic to the new primary; update security group ingress rules.

explanation: RDS Multi-AZ failover flips the CNAME of the DB instance endpoint to point to the newly promoted primary; clients that cache the resolved IP beyond the record's short TTL will keep talking to the unreachable old IP until they re-resolve DNS. B is wrong because RDS updates DNS automatically. C is wrong because non-Aurora RDS Multi-AZ also performs automatic DNS failover.

stem: A global gaming company needs a session-state store that supports low-latency reads and writes from users in North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific, with automatic multi-region active-active replication and last-writer-wins conflict resolution. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables
Amazon RDS for MySQL with cross-region read replicas
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with cross-region replication groups configured for active-active
Amazon Aurora Global Database with one writer region

explanation: DynamoDB Global Tables provide fully managed multi-region, multi-active replication with automatic last-writer-wins conflict resolution and no application-level replication logic. RDS read replicas are read-only in secondary regions, Aurora Global Database has a single writer region, and ElastiCache Global Datastore replicates one-way from a primary, none of which offer true multi-active local writes.

stem: A media company serves static assets from an S3 bucket through Amazon CloudFront. To protect against an S3 regional outage affecting the origin bucket, the company wants CloudFront to automatically serve requests from a replica bucket in a different Region if the primary origin returns errors, without manual intervention. Which feature should the DevOps engineer configure?

choices.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration on the primary bucket
CloudFront origin groups with the primary bucket as primary origin and the replicated bucket as the failover origin, combined with S3 Cross-Region Replication
A Lambda@Edge function that redirects requests when it detects a 5xx from S3
Multiple CloudFront distributions pointing to each bucket, switched via Route 53 weighted routing

explanation: CloudFront origin groups define a primary and failover origin, and CloudFront automatically retries the failover origin when the primary returns configured error codes; combined with S3 Cross-Region Replication keeping the failover bucket in sync, this gives automatic CDN-layer failover. Lambda@Edge redirects are slower and more complex, and separate distributions switched via Route 53 add DNS propagation delay.

stem: A DevOps engineer is designing a highly available web tier behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) with EC2 targets registered in three Availability Zones. What is the purpose of enabling cross-zone load balancing on the ALB's target groups in this scenario?

choices.text: It encrypts traffic between the ALB and targets across AZs.
It distributes incoming requests evenly across all registered, healthy targets in all enabled AZs, rather than only evenly across AZs regardless of how many targets are in each.
It automatically launches replacement instances in a healthy AZ if one AZ fails.
It enables the ALB to route traffic to targets in AZs where the ALB does not have a subnet.

explanation: Cross-zone load balancing ensures each load balancer node distributes traffic evenly across all registered targets in all enabled AZs, not just targets in its own AZ, preventing an AZ with fewer targets from receiving disproportionate traffic per target. It is unrelated to encryption, and instance replacement is an Auto Scaling function, not a load-balancing feature.

stem: A compliance team asks a DevOps engineer to explain the difference between Amazon S3's durability and availability design goals for the S3 Standard storage class. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Durability and availability are the same metric; both are 99.999999999% (11 nines).

Durability (designed for 99.999999999%) describes the likelihood that stored objects are not lost, while availability (designed for 99.99%) describes the percentage of time the service is expected to be accessible; a highly durable object can still be temporarily unavailable.
S3 Standard has lower durability than S3 One Zone-IA but higher availability.
Availability is guaranteed at 100% because S3 stores data redundantly across multiple devices in a single Availability Zone.

explanation: S3 Standard is designed for 11 nines of durability (data is not lost) and separately for 99.99% availability (the service can be reached to serve requests) — distinct metrics, so a durable object can still be briefly unreachable. S3 One Zone-IA shares the 11-nines durability design within one AZ but has lower availability than S3 Standard, and no AWS service offers a literal 100% availability guarantee.

stem: A company uses DynamoDB Global Tables replicated across us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Two users in different regions update the same item's status attribute within milliseconds of each other while a brief network delay slows replication. After replication catches up, both regions show the same final value, but it is not necessarily the update that occurred first in real time. What explains this, and what should the team do if it is unacceptable for a given attribute?

choices.text: This indicates a bug; open a support case, since Global Tables guarantee strict global write ordering.

DynamoDB Global Tables resolve concurrent writes with a last-writer-wins strategy based on an internal timestamp; if stricter conflict handling is required, applications should use conditional writes or version attributes, or avoid concurrent multi-region writes to that item.
Enable DynamoDB Streams to automatically enforce strict cross-region consistency.
Switch to DynamoDB Transactions, which are natively conflict-free across Global Tables regions.

explanation: Global Tables use last-writer-wins conflict resolution based on an internal timestamp, so the winning write is not guaranteed to match real-world ordering intuition for near-simultaneous writes — this is documented, expected behavior, not a bug. Applications needing stricter semantics must design around it (conditional writes, versioning, avoiding concurrent cross-region writes); Streams and Transactions do not eliminate this cross-region conflict resolution.

stem: A financial services company runs an active-passive architecture across two Regions with several interdependent Route 53 health checks controlling failover for multiple services. During a recent test, engineers manually toggling individual health checks caused a partial, inconsistent failover where some services pointed to the new Region while others did not, increasing cross-region calls and latency. Which capability is purpose-built to coordinate multi-service failover as a single, auditable action across Regions?

choices.text: AWS Config conformance packs
Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (Route 53 ARC), using routing controls and safety rules to coordinate failover atomically
AWS Systems Manager Automation documents triggered independently per service
Increasing the Route 53 health check interval to reduce flapping

explanation: Route 53 ARC provides routing controls, readiness checks, and safety rules that let teams manage and audit coordinated failover across multiple resources and Regions as controlled actions, preventing the kind of partial, inconsistent failover described. Config conformance packs address compliance, independent per-service Automation runs lack built-in cross-service coordination, and changing the health check interval does not solve the coordination problem.

stem: A DevOps engineer is designing cross-AZ load balancing for a fleet of gRPC microservices that require full-duplex, long-lived TCP connections with the lowest possible latency, and do not need Layer 7 content-based routing. Which load balancer type is the MOST appropriate choice?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer (ALB), for its Layer 7 routing capabilities
Network Load Balancer (NLB), for its Layer 4 performance, static IP support, and ability to handle high throughput with very low latency
Classic Load Balancer, because it supports both Layer 4 and Layer 7
Gateway Load Balancer, since it is designed for high-throughput data plane appliances

explanation: NLB operates at Layer 4, delivering ultra-low latency and high throughput for long-lived TCP/UDP/TLS connections and gRPC over TCP. Since content-based routing is unneeded, ALB's extra Layer 7 processing is unnecessary overhead. Classic Load Balancer is a legacy option not recommended for new workloads, and Gateway Load Balancer targets third-party virtual appliances, not application traffic.

stem: A DevOps engineer is evaluating Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments (with two readable standby instances) versus a traditional Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment (single standby, not readable) for a MySQL workload that needs both HA and the ability to offload read traffic without provisioning separate read replicas. Which statement correctly compares the two?

choices.text: Both deployment types allow read traffic to be served from standby instances.

Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments use two readable standby replicas with a dedicated reader endpoint and typically faster failover, while a traditional Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has a single, non-readable standby used only for failover.
Traditional Multi-AZ DB instance deployments always fail over faster than Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments.
Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments are only available for Aurora, not for RDS for MySQL or PostgreSQL.

explanation: RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments (supported for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and MariaDB) provide one writer and two readable standbys with a dedicated reader endpoint, typically achieving faster failover than the traditional single, non-readable-standby Multi-AZ instance deployment. This RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster feature is distinct from Aurora's own Multi-AZ model.

stem: An architecture chains three services for every request: an API Gateway/Lambda tier (99.95% SLA), an ALB/ECS tier (99.99% SLA), and a single-AZ RDS instance (no Multi-AZ, treated as ~99.5% available). A DevOps engineer is asked why the end-to-end availability is far lower than any individual component's SLA. What is the correct explanation and the BEST first remediation step?

choices.text: AWS SLAs are additive, so end-to-end availability is the sum of the three percentages; no remediation is needed since the sum exceeds 100%.

For components combined in series, combined availability is approximately the product of each component's availability, always lower than the weakest link; the highest-leverage fix is enabling Multi-AZ on the RDS instance, the least available component in the chain.
End-to-end availability is determined only by the least reliable component and is unaffected by the number of components in the chain.
Because API Gateway and Lambda are serverless, they should be excluded from the availability calculation entirely.

explanation: For a serial dependency chain, combined availability is approximately the product of each component's individual availability (0.9995 x 0.9999 x 0.995 is roughly 99.39%), lower than any single stated SLA, which is why architects must consider composite availability. The single-AZ RDS instance is the weakest link, so converting it to Multi-AZ delivers the largest improvement; SLAs are not additive and every component in the chain affects overall availability.

stem: An ECS service running on Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer experiences request latency spikes during traffic surges because new tasks take too long to become healthy. The DevOps engineer wants the service to scale out proactively based on load rather than reactively after CPU is already saturated. Which Application Auto Scaling configuration BEST achieves this for the ECS service?

choices.text: A step scaling policy based on CPUUtilization with a single large step
A target tracking scaling policy based on the ALBRequestCountPerTarget metric, set to a target value that keeps per-task request load below the point where added latency appears
Scheduled scaling actions based on historical peak hours only
Manually adjusting desired count via the AWS CLI whenever CloudWatch shows elevated latency

explanation: Target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget scales based on the actual request load each task handles, which more directly reflects capacity needs for latency-sensitive, request-driven workloads than CPU-based step scaling, and reacts continuously. Scheduled scaling and manual CLI adjustments cannot respond to unpredictable surges.

stem: A DevOps engineer manages an Amazon EKS cluster with highly variable, spiky workloads that require diverse instance types and rapid provisioning of right-sized nodes, including Spot Instances and bin-packing efficiency. The team is deciding between the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler (using EC2 Auto Scaling groups) and Karpenter. Which statement correctly compares them for this use case?

choices.text: Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter are functionally identical; the choice is purely a licensing decision.

Karpenter provisions nodes directly and dynamically based on aggregate pending pod requirements, selecting flexible instance types for efficient bin-packing without requiring pre-defined Auto Scaling groups per instance type, generally scaling faster and more efficiently than Cluster Autoscaler for diverse, spiky workloads.
Cluster Autoscaler supports Spot Instances natively while Karpenter does not support Spot at all.
Karpenter can only run outside of EKS and is incompatible with AWS-managed Kubernetes control planes.

explanation: Karpenter observes unschedulable pods and directly launches right-sized EC2 instances (mixed types, Spot or On-Demand) without pre-provisioned Auto Scaling groups per instance type/AZ, generally scaling faster and packing more efficiently than Cluster Autoscaler, which scales pre-defined node groups. Both tools support Spot Instances, and Karpenter is fully compatible with Amazon EKS.

stem: A public API built with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda begins returning HTTP 429 errors to clients during a traffic spike, even though the Lambda function's concurrency metrics show it is well under its account concurrency limit. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The Lambda function's reserved concurrency is set too high.
API Gateway's account-level or configured throttling limits (steady-state rate and burst limits) are being exceeded before requests reach Lambda.
The API Gateway REST API is missing a usage plan, which is mandatory for all APIs.
Lambda's dead-letter queue is full, rejecting new invocations.

explanation: API Gateway enforces its own throttling limits independent of Lambda concurrency; when the incoming rate exceeds these limits, API Gateway returns 429 directly without invoking Lambda, matching Lambda's low concurrency utilization. Usage plans are optional, Lambda's DLQ applies to async invocations and does not cause API Gateway 429s, and high reserved concurrency alone would not cause this pattern.

stem: A latency-sensitive Lambda function suffers from cold-start delays right after deployment and during sudden traffic bursts, even though overall workload volume is fairly predictable. Which Lambda scaling configuration is the MOST direct fix, and how does it differ from simply increasing reserved concurrency?

choices.text: Reserved concurrency, because it pre-initializes execution environments to eliminate cold starts.

Provisioned concurrency, because it keeps a specified number of execution environments initialized and ready, unlike reserved concurrency, which only guarantees/limits maximum concurrent executions without pre-warming any environments.
Increasing the function's memory allocation, since memory and concurrency are the same setting in Lambda.
Enabling Lambda SnapStart, which is supported for all Lambda runtimes equally and removes the need for either concurrency setting.

explanation: Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments so invocations are served immediately, directly reducing cold starts. Reserved concurrency only caps/reserves concurrency capacity without pre-warming anything. Memory and concurrency are separate settings, and SnapStart's runtime support and benefits are more limited than a universal replacement for these settings.

stem: A DevOps engineer is deciding whether to enable caching on an Amazon API Gateway REST API stage versus relying solely on Amazon CloudFront caching in front of the API for a public, read-heavy endpoint. Which consideration is MOST relevant to this decision?

choices.text: API Gateway caching and CloudFront caching are mutually exclusive and cannot be used together.

API Gateway stage caching operates close to the backend integration with a configurable per-stage TTL, reducing backend load, while CloudFront caching operates at edge locations closer to users, reducing latency and API Gateway request costs; the two can be combined for layered caching.
CloudFront cannot cache API Gateway origins because API Gateway does not support HTTP.
Only CloudFront caching can be configured with a TTL; API Gateway caching always uses a fixed, non-configurable 300-second TTL.

explanation: API Gateway stage caching reduces calls to backend integrations with a configurable TTL, while CloudFront caching sits at edge locations globally, reducing end-user latency and offloading API Gateway traffic; combining both provides layered benefits and they are not mutually exclusive. API Gateway supports HTTP(S) and can be a CloudFront origin, and its cache TTL is configurable, not fixed.

stem: A DevOps engineer configures Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling predictive scaling for a workload with a strong, recurring daily traffic pattern. What does predictive scaling add compared to using only dynamic (e.g., target tracking) scaling policies?

choices.text: It replaces the need for any minimum or maximum capacity settings on the Auto Scaling group.

It forecasts expected load using machine learning based on historical CloudWatch metrics and proactively schedules capacity ahead of anticipated demand, complementing dynamic scaling, which reacts to real-time metric changes after they occur.
It guarantees zero scaling latency by pre-launching every possible instance type in advance.
It is only usable with Spot Instances, not On-Demand capacity.

explanation: Predictive scaling uses machine learning on historical patterns to forecast future demand and scale out ahead of the predicted need, addressing the lag inherent in reactive dynamic scaling. It does not remove min/max capacity bounds, is not restricted to Spot Instances, and does not pre-launch every instance type.

stem: An Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions (duration-based cookies) enabled distributes traffic to an Auto Scaling group backing a stateful web application. After a scale-in event terminates several instances, many users are abruptly logged out and see inconsistent cart contents. What is the BEST long-term fix, rather than simply disabling sticky sessions?

choices.text: Increase the sticky session cookie duration to 7 days so sessions rarely expire.

Externalize session state to a shared, resilient store (such as ElastiCache for Redis or DynamoDB) so any instance can serve any user's session, removing the dependency on a specific instance surviving scale-in.
Disable Auto Scaling entirely to prevent instance termination.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to never terminate instances that currently have active sticky sessions.

explanation: The root problem is that session state lives only on individual instances; externalizing it to a shared store like ElastiCache or DynamoDB makes the application stateless at the instance level so scaling and failover do not disrupt sessions. Longer cookie duration only delays the issue, disabling Auto Scaling sacrifices elasticity, and blocking termination of sessioned instances undermines scale-in and is operationally impractical.

stem: A DevOps engineer must choose between a step scaling policy and a target tracking scaling policy for an Auto Scaling group backing a workload where the relationship between load and required capacity is well understood and stable over time. Which is generally the recommended approach, and why?

choices.text: Step scaling, because it always reacts faster than target tracking regardless of workload.

Target tracking, because it automatically manages the scaling adjustments needed to keep a chosen metric near a target value, without requiring the engineer to define specific step adjustments for different breach magnitudes.
Step scaling, because target tracking cannot use custom CloudWatch metrics.
Neither; only scheduled scaling should be used for stable, well-understood workloads.

explanation: Target tracking is generally recommended when the metric-to-capacity relationship is well understood, because AWS automatically calculates needed scaling adjustments rather than requiring manually defined step adjustments. Target tracking does support custom CloudWatch metrics, and scheduled scaling complements rather than replaces reactive scaling.

stem: A batch-processing fleet uses EC2 Auto Scaling and takes several minutes for each new instance to complete OS updates, agent installation, and application warm-up before it can accept work, slowing the fleet's response to sudden scale-out events. Which Auto Scaling feature reduces this effective scale-out latency by keeping pre-initialized instances in a low-cost state ready to be moved into service quickly?

choices.text: Auto Scaling warm pools, which keep pre-initialized instances in a stopped, hibernated, or running state outside the active pool, ready to be quickly moved into service when the group needs to scale out
Launch templates with larger instance types
Lifecycle hooks configured only for instance termination
Increasing the Auto Scaling group's cooldown period

explanation: Warm pools keep pre-initialized instances that have already completed lengthy bootstrap steps ready to be added to the active pool much faster than launching and initializing from scratch. Larger instance types do not reduce bootstrap time, termination-only lifecycle hooks do not address launch-time delays, and a longer cooldown period would slow, not speed up, additional scaling reactions.

stem: A team needs a caching layer in front of Amazon Aurora for a read-heavy reporting dashboard and is deciding between Amazon ElastiCache for Redis and Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached. Multi-AZ automatic failover of the cache cluster itself, and data structure operations beyond simple key-value (such as sorted sets), are both required. Which should they choose?

choices.text: ElastiCache for Memcached, because it natively supports multi-threading for higher throughput per node.
ElastiCache for Redis, because it supports advanced data structures (sorted sets, lists, hashes) and offers Multi-AZ with automatic failover, which Memcached does not provide.
Either engine is equivalent for this use case since both support Multi-AZ failover and identical data structures.
ElastiCache for Memcached, because only Memcached integrates with Aurora caching.

explanation: Redis supports rich data structures beyond key-value pairs and ElastiCache for Redis offers Multi-AZ with automatic failover; Memcached is a simpler, multi-threaded, pure key-value cache without built-in replication, failover, or advanced data structures. Neither engine has special native integration with Aurora beyond being used as an application-level cache.

stem: A public API Gateway REST API integrated with a Lambda function experiences p99 latency spikes correlated with deployments and with periods of low traffic followed by sudden bursts. CloudWatch Logs show many Lambda INIT duration entries during these spikes. Reserved concurrency is not configured. Which combination of actions will MOST effectively reduce these cold-start-driven latency spikes without overprovisioning cost during quiet periods?

choices.text: Set the function's timeout to the maximum allowed value.

Configure Application Auto Scaling to manage Lambda provisioned concurrency with a target-tracking policy tied to utilization so pre-warmed capacity scales up ahead of bursts and back down during quiet periods, and evaluate whether SnapStart applies to the runtime in use.
Set reserved concurrency equal to the account concurrency limit to guarantee no throttling.
Switch the Lambda function's architecture from arm64 to x86_64, which eliminates cold starts entirely.

explanation: Provisioned concurrency, scaled automatically via Application Auto Scaling target tracking, keeps a variable number of environments pre-initialized to reduce cold starts during bursts while shrinking during quiet periods to control cost; SnapStart can further reduce init duration where applicable. Increasing timeout does not address initialization latency, maxing out reserved concurrency does not pre-warm environments and can starve other functions, and changing CPU architecture does not eliminate cold starts.

stem: A DevOps engineer wants to validate that an RDS Multi-AZ deployment's automatic failover mechanism actually works and that the application reconnects correctly, without waiting for an actual infrastructure failure. Which action safely tests this?

choices.text: Delete the standby instance from the AWS Management Console to simulate a failure.

Use the Reboot with failover option on the RDS DB instance (or the equivalent API/CLI action), which forces a failover to the standby, letting the team validate application reconnection behavior in a controlled manner.
Manually change the DB instance's DNS CNAME record to point elsewhere.
Modify the security group to block all traffic to the primary instance.

explanation: RDS provides Reboot with failover specifically to let teams safely test Multi-AZ failover on demand, forcing failover to the standby so the team can confirm DNS updates and application reconnection. Deleting the standby is destructive and not a normal failover test; manually altering DNS or blocking traffic via security groups does not exercise RDS's actual failover mechanism.

stem: A company is deciding between a backup and restore DR strategy and a pilot light DR strategy for a moderately critical application. Leadership wants to understand the cost versus recovery-time tradeoff. Which statement correctly frames this tradeoff?

choices.text: Backup and restore has the lowest cost of common DR strategies but generally the longest RTO, since infrastructure must be provisioned and data restored after a disaster is declared; pilot light costs more due to always-on core components but reduces RTO because the most time-consuming-to-restore components are already running or continuously replicated.
Backup and restore and pilot light have identical RTOs because both rely on AWS Backup.
Pilot light always costs more than a full multi-region active-active architecture.
Backup and restore is not a valid DR strategy recognized by AWS; only pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active are valid.

explanation: Backup and restore is the lowest-cost common DR strategy but typically has the longest RTO since infrastructure is built and data restored only after a disaster. Pilot light keeps critical core components running or replicated continuously, costing more at steady state but reducing RTO. AWS documents backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active as a recognized cost/RTO spectrum of DR strategies.

stem: A company operates a multi-region active-passive architecture and wants to continuously verify, before an actual disaster, that the secondary Region's resources (database connectivity, required capacity, DNS configuration) are truly ready to take over traffic at any moment, integrated with its Route 53-based failover mechanism. Which capability should the DevOps engineer implement?

choices.text: Route 53 Application Recovery Controller readiness checks, which continuously evaluate resource readiness (capacity, database status, and more) against configured rules in each Region so the team knows in advance whether failover would actually succeed
A manually run script executed once per quarter to check secondary Region status
CloudWatch billing alarms on the secondary Region
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks

explanation: Route 53 ARC readiness checks continuously audit whether resources in each Region meet defined readiness rules, giving ongoing, automated confidence that failover would succeed before a real disaster, directly matching the requirement. A quarterly manual script is not continuous, and billing alarms or Trusted Advisor cost checks are unrelated to DR readiness verification.

stem: An operations team wants a standardized, automated way to detect specific operational issues (such as an application returning high error rates) and immediately trigger a predefined, auditable remediation runbook (for example, restarting a service, rolling back a deployment, or paging the on-call engineer with diagnostic context) as part of its automated recovery process. Which AWS service is designed specifically for this incident detection-to-response workflow?

choices.text: AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager, which can be triggered by a CloudWatch alarm to automatically start a predefined incident response plan, execute Systems Manager Automation runbooks, and engage the right responders
AWS Config, which can only report on configuration drift, not trigger remediation
Amazon Inspector, which is designed for vulnerability scanning, not incident response
AWS Trusted Advisor, which only provides periodic best-practice checks

explanation: Systems Manager Incident Manager reduces time-to-resolution for operational issues: it can be triggered automatically by a CloudWatch alarm, execute a predefined incident response plan including Automation runbooks, and engage on-call responders, matching the described workflow. Config can trigger SSM Automation for remediation but is primarily a compliance service, Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, and Trusted Advisor gives periodic recommendations rather than real-time incident response.

stem: An ECS service running critical tasks occasionally has tasks that pass their ALB health check but are actually deadlocked and not processing requests, because the health check endpoint does not exercise the deadlocked code path. The team wants an automated way to detect and recover from this condition without waiting for a customer-reported incident. Which combination of actions is MOST effective?

choices.text: Rely solely on ECS's built-in task health checks, since ECS automatically detects application-level deadlocks.

Publish a custom CloudWatch metric from the application reflecting true processing health (such as queue drain rate or synthetic transaction latency), create a CloudWatch alarm on that metric, and use the alarm to trigger a Systems Manager Automation runbook (or an ECS service action) that forces replacement of the affected tasks.
Increase the ALB health check interval so unhealthy tasks are detected sooner.
Disable health checks entirely so tasks are never marked unhealthy.

explanation: Since the shallow health check does not exercise the deadlocked code path, a deeper, application-specific CloudWatch metric combined with an alarm and an automated remediation runbook that replaces the affected tasks provides real detection and recovery. Default ECS/ALB health checks do not detect application-level deadlocks by themselves, a longer interval slows detection, and disabling health checks removes the only safety net.

stem: Before relying on its documented multi-AZ and multi-Region failover procedures during a real incident, a DevOps team wants to proactively and safely inject controlled failures (such as terminating a percentage of EC2 instances, injecting network latency, or simulating an AZ power interruption) into a non-production environment to validate that automated recovery mechanisms behave as expected. Which AWS service is designed for this purpose?

choices.text: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), which lets teams design and run controlled chaos engineering experiments, such as terminating instances, throttling APIs, or simulating AZ disruption, with built-in safety mechanisms like stop conditions
AWS Config, using custom rules to randomly terminate non-compliant resources
Amazon Inspector, by configuring it to actively terminate vulnerable instances it discovers
AWS CloudTrail, by replaying historical API calls to simulate failures

explanation: AWS Fault Injection Service is purpose-built for chaos engineering, letting teams run controlled experiments that inject realistic faults against a defined scope, with stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms to safely halt an experiment causing unexpected impact, ideal for validating automated recovery processes. Config and Inspector are not fault-injection tools, and CloudTrail is an API activity logging service with no fault-injection capability.

stem: A company runs a fleet of EC2 instances that generate application-level metrics such as active session counts every 10 seconds. The DevOps team wants these metrics available in CloudWatch with the finest possible granularity supported natively, without building a custom ingestion pipeline. Which approach meets this requirement?

choices.text: Install the unified CloudWatch agent, configure it to collect the metrics via StatsD, and publish them with a storage resolution of 1 second.
Write the metrics to a CloudWatch Logs log group and create a metric filter to extract them.
Publish the metrics using PutMetricData with the default 60-second storage resolution.
Use AWS X-Ray to record the metrics as annotations on trace segments.

explanation: The CloudWatch agent supports StatsD/collectd for custom application metrics and can publish them as high-resolution (1-second) custom metrics, meeting the sub-minute requirement natively. PutMetricData without StorageResolution=1 defaults to standard 60-second resolution, and metric filters only count log occurrences rather than capturing arbitrary numeric application values.

stem: An application writes JSON-formatted log lines to a CloudWatch Logs log group. The operations team wants an alarm to fire when the rate of log entries containing level ERROR exceeds 50 in a 5-minute period, without changing the application. What should they configure?

choices.text: Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter matching the ERROR pattern, publish it to a custom metric, and create a CloudWatch alarm on that metric.
Enable CloudWatch Logs Insights and schedule a saved query to run every 5 minutes using EventBridge as the sole alerting mechanism.
Create an S3 event notification that triggers when new log data is exported to S3.
Configure a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm directly on the log group's IncomingBytes metric.

explanation: A metric filter can match a JSON pattern like level equals ERROR and increment a custom metric, on which a standard threshold alarm can then be set. Logs Insights queries are ad hoc and not the native continuous alarming mechanism, and IncomingBytes anomaly detection would not reflect error-level semantics.

stem: A company needs near real time full text search and visualization of application logs from over 50 CloudWatch Logs log groups across multiple accounts, while retaining the ability to run ad hoc SQL-like queries on raw logs later. Which architecture best satisfies both near-real-time search and long-term ad hoc querying with minimal operational overhead?

choices.text: Subscribe each log group to a centralized Kinesis Data Stream via subscription filters, process records with a Lambda function that indexes them into Amazon OpenSearch Service for near-real-time search, and also deliver the raw records to S3 for later querying with Amazon Athena.
Export each log group nightly to S3 using the CreateExportTask API, then query the exports with Athena.
Enable CloudWatch Logs Insights on every log group and grant the visualization team direct query access.
Use CloudWatch metric streams to send log data to Kinesis Data Firehose and store it in Redshift.
