explanation: Cross-account subscription filters feeding a centralized Kinesis stream is the standard pattern for aggregating logs, and fanning out from there to OpenSearch for search/visualization and S3/Athena for ad hoc historical queries satisfies both requirements using managed services. Nightly export tasks are not near-real-time, and metric streams only carry CloudWatch metrics, not log data.

stem: A DevOps engineer associates a customer managed KMS key with a CloudWatch Logs log group to encrypt log data at rest. Shortly afterward, the application role that writes to the log group starts failing with AccessDenied errors when calling PutLogEvents, although it previously worked and its IAM policy grants logs:PutLogEvents on the log group. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The KMS key policy does not grant the necessary kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt, and kms:GenerateDataKey permissions to the CloudWatch Logs service principal for that region.
CloudWatch Logs log groups cannot be encrypted with customer managed KMS keys, only AWS managed keys.
The log group retention period must be set to Never expire before encryption can be enabled.
PutLogEvents requires the caller to have direct kms:Decrypt permission on the key, which IAM roles cannot be granted.

explanation: When a customer managed key is associated with a log group, the key policy must allow the logs.<region>.amazonaws.com service principal to use the key on behalf of callers; otherwise writes and reads fail even if the caller's IAM policy is correct. CloudWatch Logs does support customer managed KMS keys, and retention settings are unrelated to encryption.

stem: A company must retain application logs for 7 years for compliance but wants to minimize storage cost. Logs are currently kept indefinitely in CloudWatch Logs. Which combination of actions is the most cost-effective way to meet the retention requirement?

choices.text: Set the CloudWatch Logs log group retention policy to a shorter period, export older logs to S3, and configure an S3 lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and expire them after 7 years.
Leave the log group retention set to Never expire and rely on CloudWatch Logs' built-in low-cost archival tier.
Set the log group retention to 7 years and enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering directly on the log group.
Delete the log group every 30 days and recreate it to avoid storage charges.

explanation: CloudWatch Logs has no built-in archival tier or direct S3 tiering; the standard pattern is to shorten log group retention, export to S3, and use S3 lifecycle rules to move data to cheaper storage classes like Glacier Deep Archive before final expiration. Keeping logs in CloudWatch Logs indefinitely is far more expensive at scale, and log groups cannot have S3 storage classes applied directly to them.

stem: A monitoring team wants to continuously forward all CloudWatch metrics across an account to a third-party observability platform with near-real-time delivery and minimal custom code, and they want the solution to scale automatically as new metrics are published without per-metric configuration. Which feature should they use?

choices.text: CloudWatch metric streams delivered through Kinesis Data Firehose to the third-party endpoint.
CloudWatch Logs subscription filters forwarding to a Lambda function that republishes metrics.
A scheduled Lambda function that calls GetMetricData every minute for each metric and forwards results via HTTPS.
CloudWatch dashboards shared publicly with the third-party platform.

explanation: CloudWatch metric streams provide a near-continuous, near-real-time stream of metric updates for an account, optionally filtered by namespace, via Kinesis Data Firehose, without needing to enumerate individual metrics. Subscription filters apply to Logs, not metrics, and polling GetMetricData does not scale automatically and adds latency and API costs.

stem: A SaaS provider publishes custom CloudWatch metrics for API latency per tenant and wants to be able to view latency aggregated across all tenants, as well as drill down to an individual tenant, without publishing duplicate metric data. How should the metric be structured?

choices.text: Publish a single metric named ApiLatency in a custom namespace with a TenantId dimension, and rely on CloudWatch's dimension rollup by querying without the dimension to view account-wide aggregates.
Publish a separate metric name for every tenant, such as ApiLatency-TenantA and ApiLatency-TenantB, in the same namespace.
Publish the metric twice for each data point: once with the TenantId dimension and once without any dimensions.
Store latency values only in CloudWatch Logs and use Logs Insights to compute aggregates on demand instead of using metrics.

explanation: CloudWatch metrics with the same name and namespace but different dimension sets are treated as distinct metrics; querying with the TenantId dimension isolates one tenant, while CloudWatch's automatic dimension rollup provides an aggregate view without duplicate publishing. Publishing a separate metric per tenant or duplicating data points wastes cost and complicates aggregation.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to find, across the last 24 hours, the 10 slowest requests recorded in a log group where each log entry contains a JSON field named durationMs. Which CloudWatch Logs Insights query accomplishes this?

choices.text: fields @timestamp, durationMs, @message | sort durationMs desc | limit 10
fields @timestamp, durationMs | filter durationMs > 0 | stats count() by durationMs
parse @message "durationMs" | display @timestamp | limit 10
fields @timestamp | stats avg(durationMs) as avgDuration

explanation: Logs Insights supports sorting extracted fields and limiting results, so sorting by durationMs in descending order and limiting to 10 returns the slowest individual requests. The stats-based options aggregate data across records rather than surfacing individual slow requests.

stem: A serverless application running on AWS Lambda needs to emit custom business metrics, such as order value, alongside structured logs, without making separate PutMetricData API calls that could add latency and throttling risk to the request path. Which approach is best?

choices.text: Write log entries using the CloudWatch embedded metric format (EMF) so CloudWatch Logs automatically extracts the specified fields as custom metrics.
Call PutMetricData synchronously within the Lambda handler for every order processed.
Enable CloudWatch Container Insights for the Lambda function.
Use AWS X-Ray annotations to store the order value and later export trace data to CloudWatch metrics.

explanation: The embedded metric format lets a Lambda function log structured JSON that CloudWatch Logs automatically parses into custom metrics asynchronously, avoiding extra synchronous API calls and their latency and throttling impact. Synchronous PutMetricData calls add latency to the request path, and X-Ray annotations are for tracing, not metric extraction.

stem: A large organization with 40 AWS accounts wants all application logs centralized into one security account for analysis, while keeping each account responsible for its own log group configuration and avoiding cross-account IAM role assumption for every log delivery. Which design best meets these constraints?

choices.text: In each member account, create a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter on the relevant log groups that sends data to a Kinesis Data Stream owned by the security account, using a resource policy on the destination that permits cross-account delivery.
In the security account, assume an IAM role in each of the 40 accounts every few minutes to call FilterLogEvents and copy results locally.
Require every member account to manually export logs to S3 nightly and email the security team a summary.
Enable AWS Organizations consolidated billing, which automatically aggregates all CloudWatch Logs data into the management account.

explanation: Cross-account subscription filters push log data from each account directly to a centralized Kinesis stream via a destination resource policy, avoiding per-account role assumption and giving the security account real-time centralized data while each account keeps its own log group settings. Polling with assumed roles is operationally heavy and not near-real-time, and consolidated billing has nothing to do with log aggregation.

stem: An EC2 instance running the unified CloudWatch agent is supposed to publish custom memory and disk usage metrics, but no data appears under the CWAgent namespace in CloudWatch. The agent process is running and its configuration file passes validation. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: Whether the instance profile's IAM role includes permissions for cloudwatch:PutMetricData, and ssm:GetParameter if the configuration is stored in Parameter Store.
Whether the EC2 instance has a public IP address assigned.
Whether AWS CloudTrail is enabled in the region.
Whether the instance is part of an Auto Scaling group.

explanation: The CloudWatch agent needs an IAM role or instance profile with cloudwatch:PutMetricData permission, and SSM read access if pulling its configuration from Parameter Store, to publish metrics; missing permissions are the most common cause of a running agent producing no visible data. Public IP assignment, CloudTrail, and Auto Scaling membership are unrelated to metric publication.

stem: A cost review reveals that CloudWatch Logs storage charges have grown steadily for a year even though log volume per day is stable. Investigation shows several log groups were created by default with no retention policy set. What is the effect of this configuration, and what should be changed?

choices.text: Log events are retained indefinitely by default, so the engineer should set an explicit retention period, such as 30 or 90 days, on each affected log group to expire old data.
Log events are automatically deleted after 30 days by default, so no change is needed; the cost growth must come from another source.
CloudWatch Logs automatically compresses log data older than 90 days, so retention settings do not affect storage cost.
The log groups must be re-encrypted with a customer managed KMS key to enable automatic expiration.

explanation: When no retention policy is configured, CloudWatch Logs stores log events indefinitely, so storage costs accumulate over time; setting an explicit retention period causes old events to expire automatically. CloudWatch Logs does not delete data after 30 days by default, and encryption settings have no effect on retention or expiration behavior.

stem: A team is deciding whether to publish a custom metric at standard 60-second resolution or high 1-second resolution. The metric drives an alarm that must detect and react to spikes within 30 seconds, but the team is also concerned about cost. What is the correct trade-off consideration?

choices.text: High-resolution metrics enable alarms to evaluate on periods as short as 10 seconds, which is necessary to detect the spike within 30 seconds, but they incur higher CloudWatch custom metric costs than standard-resolution metrics.
Standard-resolution metrics can be evaluated by alarms with a 10-second period just as effectively as high-resolution metrics, so there is no reason to use high resolution.
Metric resolution only affects how metrics are displayed on dashboards and has no effect on alarm evaluation periods.
High-resolution metrics are always cheaper because they generate smaller individual data points.

explanation: Alarms on standard-resolution 60-second metrics can only evaluate on periods of 60 seconds or multiples of it, so detecting a spike within 30 seconds requires high-resolution 1-second metrics with a supported short period, at a higher publishing cost. Resolution directly affects the minimum alarm evaluation period, not just dashboard display.

stem: An e-commerce platform's request count metric naturally varies by time of day and day of week. The operations team wants to be alerted only when traffic deviates significantly from the expected pattern for that specific time, rather than using a single static threshold. Which CloudWatch feature should they use?

choices.text: CloudWatch anomaly detection, which models expected metric behavior based on historical data and can trigger an alarm when the metric falls outside the predicted band.
A static threshold alarm set to the highest observed value from the past month.
An AWS Config custom rule that evaluates the metric hourly.
A CloudWatch Logs Insights scheduled query with a fixed numeric filter.

explanation: CloudWatch anomaly detection builds a model of expected values, including daily and weekly seasonality, and alarms when the metric falls outside the computed band, which fits variable traffic patterns better than one static threshold. A single static threshold set to the peak value would miss legitimate anomalies during low-traffic periods.

stem: A security analyst needs to run ad hoc SQL queries against a year of CloudTrail logs stored as compressed JSON files in S3 to identify all IAM console logins from a specific IP range, without provisioning a database server. What is the most appropriate service?

choices.text: Amazon Athena, using a table defined over the CloudTrail S3 location, optionally via the built-in CloudTrail SerDe, to run SQL queries directly against the log files.
Amazon RDS, by importing the CloudTrail JSON files into a relational database schema first.
CloudWatch Logs Insights, after manually re-uploading a year of CloudTrail data into a log group.
AWS Config, by creating a custom rule that evaluates historical login events.

explanation: Athena is a serverless interactive query service that can query CloudTrail logs directly in S3 using SQL, and AWS provides guidance and table definitions, including a CloudTrail SerDe, specifically for this use case, requiring no server provisioning or data movement. Importing a year of logs into RDS or re-uploading into CloudWatch Logs is unnecessary operational overhead.

stem: An executive team wants a polished, interactive business-facing dashboard showing trends derived from operational CloudWatch metrics and log-derived KPIs, with role-based access control and the ability to embed the dashboard in an internal web portal. Which service is best suited to build this dashboard, compared to a native CloudWatch dashboard?

choices.text: Amazon QuickSight, which provides rich BI visualizations, row-level security, and embedding capabilities beyond what native CloudWatch dashboards offer.
A native CloudWatch dashboard, since it already supports embedding in external portals with fine-grained row-level security.
AWS Config aggregator dashboards, which are designed for executive-level KPI reporting.
Amazon Inspector findings reports, which can be converted directly into BI dashboards.

explanation: QuickSight is a BI service designed for polished, interactive dashboards with granular access control and embedding into applications or portals, making it a better fit for executive-facing reporting than CloudWatch dashboards, which are primarily operational and lack row-level security and embedding sophistication. Config and Inspector are not BI or dashboarding services.

stem: A high-throughput API instrumented with AWS X-Ray is generating very high tracing costs due to the default sampling behavior capturing a large volume of routine successful requests. The team wants to reduce the volume of traces recorded for high-volume, low-value routes while still retaining visibility into overall system behavior. What should they configure?

choices.text: Custom X-Ray sampling rules that set a lower fixed rate and smaller reservoir for the high-volume, low-priority routes, while keeping a higher sampling rate for critical routes.
Disable X-Ray tracing entirely and rely solely on CloudWatch metrics for latency and errors.
Increase the default sampling rate to 100 percent to guarantee no traces are missed, accepting the cost increase.
Move all tracing data collection to CloudTrail data events instead of X-Ray.

explanation: X-Ray sampling rules can be scoped by attributes such as service name, HTTP method, and URL path, letting teams apply a lower reservoir and rate to high-volume, low-priority routes to cut tracing volume and cost while keeping richer sampling for critical paths. Disabling tracing loses request-level visibility entirely, and CloudTrail data events record management or data plane API calls, not distributed application tracing.

stem: A company wants to automatically detect unusual patterns in management API call volume, such as a sudden spike in IAM role creation calls that could indicate compromised credentials, without building custom anomaly-detection logic. Which CloudTrail feature addresses this?

choices.text: CloudTrail Insights, which analyzes management event activity and automatically surfaces unusual API call volume or error rate patterns.
CloudTrail log file integrity validation, which detects unusual API call patterns via digest file signatures.
Standard CloudTrail event history, which by default flags anomalous call volumes.
AWS Config resource timeline, which highlights anomalous configuration change frequency.

explanation: CloudTrail Insights automatically analyzes trail activity and identifies unusual patterns, such as spikes in API call volume or error rates, that could indicate operational or security issues, without requiring custom anomaly-detection code. Log file integrity validation is about tamper detection, not anomaly detection, and plain event history does not perform automated anomaly analysis.

stem: A team needs to compute a running aggregate, such as a rolling error rate, from application log events with sub-second latency to drive an automated scaling decision, continuously and in real time. They are deciding between streaming the logs through Kinesis Data Streams with a custom consumer application, versus periodically running CloudWatch Logs Insights queries. Which factor most strongly favors Kinesis Data Streams for this use case?

choices.text: Kinesis Data Streams enables continuous, low-latency stream processing of records as they arrive, whereas Logs Insights queries are run on demand or on a schedule against already-stored log data and are not designed for continuous sub-second stream processing.
Logs Insights cannot query numeric fields, so it is unsuitable for computing error rates.
Kinesis Data Streams is cheaper than Logs Insights for any query pattern.
CloudWatch Logs Insights automatically triggers Auto Scaling actions, making Kinesis unnecessary.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams supports continuous real-time stream processing, ideal for driving low-latency automated decisions, while Logs Insights is a query engine invoked on demand or on a schedule against stored logs and introduces query-cycle latency unsuitable for sub-second continuous aggregation. Logs Insights can handle numeric fields, and neither service triggers Auto Scaling directly.

stem: A security investigation requires determining exactly which IAM principal read a specific sensitive object from an S3 bucket last week, but the CloudTrail event history in the console shows no matching GetObject event. What is the most likely explanation, and what should be enabled going forward?

choices.text: By default, CloudTrail trails only log management events; S3 object-level API activity, known as data events, must be explicitly enabled for the bucket to capture GetObject calls.
CloudTrail never records S3 activity under any configuration; VPC Flow Logs must be used instead.
The event was not logged because the S3 bucket does not have versioning enabled.
CloudTrail only retains events for 24 hours by default, so last week's event has already expired from all storage.

explanation: CloudTrail trails log management events by default, but object-level operations like S3 GetObject and PutObject are data events that must be explicitly enabled, per bucket or account-wide, to be captured; without that, no record of the GetObject call exists. CloudTrail can log S3 activity when data events are enabled, and this is unrelated to bucket versioning or the separate 90-day console event history limit.

stem: A data pipeline needs to automatically start a Lambda function whenever a new object is uploaded to a specific S3 prefix, and the team also wants the flexibility to later route the same event to multiple additional targets, such as an SNS topic and a Step Functions workflow, without modifying the S3 bucket configuration each time. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Configure the S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge, then create EventBridge rules that route the event to the Lambda function and, later, to additional targets as needed.
Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke the Lambda function directly, and add a second, third, and fourth S3 notification configuration each time a new target is needed.
Use AWS Config to detect new S3 objects and invoke Lambda through a Config rule.
Poll the S3 bucket every minute using a scheduled Lambda function to check for new objects.

explanation: Enabling EventBridge as the S3 event destination lets a single event feed multiple EventBridge rules and targets, such as Lambda, SNS, and Step Functions, without reconfiguring the S3 bucket for each new consumer, providing flexible fan-out. Directly wiring S3 notifications to Lambda works for a single target but requires bucket-level changes to add more consumers, and polling is inefficient and slow.

stem: An operations team receives separate CloudWatch alarms for high CPU, high memory, and elevated error rate on the same application, and every incident triggers three separate pages even though they represent one underlying problem. What CloudWatch feature can reduce alert noise by combining these into a single alarm state based on a Boolean rule across the three alarms?

choices.text: A CloudWatch composite alarm that uses AND, OR, or NOT logic over the states of the three existing alarms to generate one combined alarm state.
A CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm applied to all three metrics simultaneously.
An SNS topic with three subscriptions, one per alarm, configured to deduplicate messages.
A single metric filter that merges the three underlying log-based metrics into one CloudWatch Logs Insights query.

explanation: CloudWatch composite alarms combine the alarm states of multiple existing alarms using AND, OR, and NOT rule expressions, producing a single higher-level alarm and notification when the specified condition is met, reducing duplicate pages for one underlying incident. Anomaly detection and SNS deduplication do not combine alarm logic across separate alarms.

stem: A production RDS for PostgreSQL database occasionally experiences unpredictable storage growth, and the team wants to avoid running out of allocated storage without manually monitoring free storage space and issuing modify-instance calls. What RDS feature addresses this directly?

choices.text: RDS Storage Auto Scaling, which automatically increases allocated storage when free space falls below a threshold and usage patterns indicate more capacity is needed.
Multi-AZ deployment, which automatically expands storage during failover.
RDS Performance Insights, which reallocates storage based on query performance metrics.
A CloudWatch alarm on FreeStorageSpace that must manually trigger a support ticket for AWS to expand storage.

explanation: RDS Storage Auto Scaling automatically increases allocated storage for supported engines when free storage drops below a threshold and other conditions are met, without manual intervention. Multi-AZ addresses availability, not proactive storage growth, and Performance Insights is a monitoring tool for query and database performance, not storage capacity management.

stem: A DynamoDB table serves a workload with highly unpredictable and spiky traffic, including occasional traffic that can jump 10x within seconds. The team wants to minimize throttling risk without manually forecasting capacity, and cost predictability is a secondary concern. Compared to DynamoDB auto scaling with provisioned capacity, what is the key advantage of using on-demand capacity mode here?

choices.text: On-demand capacity mode instantly accommodates sudden traffic spikes without needing to react to a scaling policy, whereas provisioned capacity with auto scaling adjusts capacity based on utilization metrics and may lag behind very sudden spikes, risking throttling.
On-demand capacity mode is always cheaper than provisioned capacity with auto scaling for any workload pattern.
Auto scaling with provisioned capacity reacts to traffic changes faster than on-demand mode in all cases.
On-demand capacity mode requires CloudWatch alarms to adjust capacity, just like provisioned auto scaling.

explanation: DynamoDB on-demand mode scales instantly to accommodate traffic without relying on CloudWatch-alarm-driven scaling actions, making it better suited to sudden, unpredictable spikes, while provisioned auto scaling reacts to utilization changes with some lag and can throttle during very rapid spikes. On-demand is typically more expensive at steady high volume, so it is not always cheaper.

stem: An ECS service configured with Service Auto Scaling using a target tracking policy on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization is not scaling out even though CloudWatch shows sustained CPU utilization above the target value. Application Auto Scaling shows the scalable target is registered correctly. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: The service has reached its configured maximum task count for the scalable target, so Application Auto Scaling cannot add more tasks despite the metric exceeding the target.
ECS services cannot be scaled based on CPU utilization; only memory-based metrics are supported.
Target tracking policies for ECS require a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter to function.
The ECS cluster must be using EC2 launch type; Fargate services cannot use target tracking scaling.

explanation: Application Auto Scaling will not scale a service beyond the MinCapacity or MaxCapacity bounds configured on the scalable target, so if MaxCapacity is already reached, no further scale-out occurs even with sustained high CPU. ECS supports both CPU and memory target tracking metrics, and target tracking works on both EC2 and Fargate launch types.

stem: A CloudWatch alarm monitors disk space on a fleet of EC2 instances and needs to automatically run a cleanup script on the affected instance when it enters ALARM state, in addition to notifying the on-call engineer. Which design achieves automated remediation and notification together?

choices.text: Configure the alarm to publish to an SNS topic with two subscriptions: one delivering email or SMS to the on-call engineer, and one invoking a Lambda function that uses Systems Manager Run Command to execute the cleanup script on the affected instance.
Configure the alarm to invoke AWS Config directly, which will run the cleanup script as a remediation action.
Configure the alarm to write to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and rely on a metric filter to run the cleanup script.
Configure the alarm to trigger an EC2 Auto Scaling scheduled action that reboots the instance nightly.

explanation: An SNS topic can fan out an alarm notification to both a human-facing subscription and a Lambda function subscription that triggers remediation, such as invoking SSM Run Command to execute a script on the instance, achieving both notification and automated remediation. CloudWatch alarms do not invoke AWS Config or run scripts directly, and a nightly reboot does not target the alarm condition specifically.

stem: A company wants any EC2 instance found by an AWS Config rule to be missing the required CloudWatch agent installation to be automatically remediated by installing and starting the agent via Systems Manager, without manual operator action. Which configuration accomplishes this?

choices.text: Attach a remediation configuration to the Config rule that specifies an SSM Automation document, such as one using Run Command to install and start the CloudWatch agent, and enable automatic remediation.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the Config rule's compliance metric that emails the operations team to manually install the agent.
Use AWS Config to directly install software on noncompliant resources without any SSM integration.
Enable AWS Systems Manager Inventory, which automatically installs missing agents when it detects them.

explanation: AWS Config remediation configurations let you attach an SSM Automation document to a rule and enable automatic remediation, so noncompliant resources are corrected, such as installing the CloudWatch agent, without manual steps. AWS Config itself cannot execute remediation actions without an Automation document, and SSM Inventory only collects inventory data, it does not install software automatically.

stem: An Application Load Balancer is marking healthy EC2 targets as unhealthy and removing them from rotation during brief periods of high CPU load, even though the application recovers within a few seconds and would have served the next request successfully. Users experience intermittent 503 errors during these periods. What should be adjusted to reduce unnecessary target deregistration during brief transient slowness?

choices.text: Increase the health check UnhealthyThreshold count and, or, the health check interval and timeout so that a single brief slow response does not immediately mark the target unhealthy.
Decrease the health check interval to check more frequently, so problems are caught faster.
Remove the health check entirely so targets are never marked unhealthy.
Switch the ALB to use TCP health checks instead of HTTP health checks, which ignore application-level slowness entirely.

explanation: Increasing the unhealthy threshold and, or, the interval and timeout gives a target more tolerance for transient slow responses before being deregistered, reducing false-positive unhealthy markings from brief CPU spikes. Decreasing the interval makes the load balancer more sensitive, not less, and removing health checks entirely would route traffic to genuinely failed targets.

stem: A team currently uses EventBridge rules with cron expressions to trigger Lambda functions on fixed schedules, but as the number of scheduled jobs grows into the thousands across accounts, they hit default EventBridge rule quotas and want a purpose-built scheduling service with higher scalability, at-least-once delivery guarantees, and native support for time zones and one-time schedules. Which service should they migrate to?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, which is designed to manage a very large number of schedules with features like time zone support, flexible time windows, and one-time or recurring invocations, separate from EventBridge rule quotas.
AWS Config scheduled rules, which are designed for high-scale job scheduling.
CloudWatch Logs scheduled queries, which can invoke Lambda functions on a cron schedule at any scale.
Amazon Inspector scheduled scans, repurposed to invoke arbitrary Lambda functions.

explanation: EventBridge Scheduler is a dedicated scheduling service built to scale to a very large number of schedules with features like time zones, flexible time windows, and one-time schedules, and it operates independently of the older EventBridge rule-based scheduling quotas. AWS Config scheduled rules and CloudWatch Logs scheduled queries are not general-purpose job schedulers, and Amazon Inspector scans are unrelated to scheduling arbitrary functions.

stem: A team is considering enabling automatic remediation on an AWS Config rule that terminates EC2 instances launched with unencrypted EBS volumes. What is the primary risk of enabling fully automatic remediation for this specific rule compared to manual approval-based remediation?

choices.text: An automatic remediation that terminates instances could unexpectedly destroy production workloads or data if the rule logic or remediation action is misconfigured or triggers on a false positive, whereas requiring manual approval provides a safety check before a destructive action executes.
AWS Config does not support automatic remediation for EBS-related rules, so this option is not available regardless of risk.
Automatic remediation always requires the target instance to already be terminated, so there is no additional risk.
Manual remediation approval is not supported by AWS Config, making this comparison invalid.

explanation: For destructive remediation actions, automatic execution removes the human checkpoint that would otherwise catch a misconfigured rule, an overly broad remediation, or a false-positive evaluation before it destroys a production resource; AWS Config does support requiring manual execution or approval of a remediation action as a safer alternative. AWS Config does support automatic remediation generally, including custom SSM documents that could terminate instances, so the claim that it is unavailable is incorrect.

stem: A company runs workloads across 20 AWS accounts managed through AWS Organizations. The security team wants a single centralized location to receive AWS Health events (including scheduled maintenance and abuse notifications) from every member account without requiring each account to configure its own forwarding rule from scratch. Which approach meets this requirement with the least ongoing per-account configuration?

choices.text: Enable AWS Health organizational view in the management account, then create an EventBridge rule in the management account's default event bus matching aws.health events, and target a centralized SNS topic.
In each member account, create an EventBridge rule matching aws.health source events and configure it to send events to an SQS queue in the security account.
Enable AWS Config aggregator in the management account to collect Health events from all member accounts.
Subscribe the security team's email directly to AWS Personal Health Dashboard RSS feeds for each account.

explanation: AWS Health's organizational view (aggregation) lets the management account receive Health events for all member accounts, and a single EventBridge rule in that account can route them centrally with no per-account setup. Config aggregator handles configuration compliance data, not Health events, and per-account EventBridge rules (B) work but require configuring each account, which the question asks to avoid.

stem: A DevOps engineer configured an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function whenever a specific S3 object is deleted, matching CloudTrail's DeleteObject event. The rule works for management events like bucket policy changes but never fires for the object delete calls. What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: CloudTrail does not log S3 object-level API calls by default; the engineer must enable data events for the S3 bucket in the trail configuration.
EventBridge cannot match rules on S3 API calls; the engineer must switch to S3 Event Notifications instead.
The Lambda function's execution role lacks s3:GetObject permission.
CloudTrail only delivers events to CloudWatch Logs, not EventBridge, so the rule can never match.

explanation: CloudTrail records only management events by default; object-level (data) events such as GetObject and DeleteObject must be explicitly enabled on the trail, after which CloudTrail delivers them to EventBridge automatically. EventBridge fully supports matching on CloudTrail-sourced API events, and a Lambda execution role permission issue would cause invocation failures, not a complete absence of matching, so it does not explain the symptom.

stem: A security team wants to be alerted in near real time whenever any IAM user or role calls CreateAccessKey, and separately wants AWS to automatically detect unusual spikes in API call volume or error rates without the team having to define specific API names or thresholds to watch. Which combination of services satisfies both requirements?

choices.text: An EventBridge rule matching CreateAccessKey events for real-time alerting, plus CloudTrail Insights enabled on the trail to detect anomalous API activity patterns.
A single CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the CloudTrail log group that counts all IAM API calls and alarms on any threshold breach.
AWS Config rules evaluating IAM resource configurations on a periodic basis.
GuardDuty findings exported to EventBridge covering both use cases without any CloudTrail configuration.

explanation: An EventBridge rule with an event pattern on the specific eventName gives real-time, precise alerting for a known API call, and CloudTrail Insights automatically baselines normal API call volume and error-rate patterns to surface anomalies without predefined thresholds. Config evaluates configuration state rather than API activity, and a manual metric filter requires a fixed threshold rather than adaptive anomaly detection.

stem: An incident response pipeline uses an EventBridge rule to invoke a Lambda function directly whenever a GuardDuty finding is published. During a recent incident storm, several findings were dropped because the Lambda function's concurrency limit was reached and EventBridge's retry policy expired before capacity freed up. Which change would most effectively prevent event loss during future bursts while preserving ordering-independent processing?

choices.text: Increase Lambda reserved concurrency to an arbitrarily high value so it can never be throttled.
Change the EventBridge rule target to an SQS standard queue, and have the Lambda function poll the queue as an event source with an appropriately sized batch size and concurrency.
Reduce the EventBridge rule's maximum retry attempts to 0 so failed invocations are discarded quickly.
Switch the target from Lambda to a Step Functions Express Workflow, which does not have concurrency limits.

explanation: Adding an SQS queue between EventBridge and Lambda decouples ingestion from processing, durably buffering bursts so events are not lost when Lambda is throttled, since the SQS event source mapping retries and scales consumption as capacity allows. Raising concurrency indefinitely is costly and can still be exceeded, reducing retries discards events faster, and Express Workflows are still subject to underlying account and service limits.

stem: A company's fleet of thousands of edge devices generates security telemetry that must be ingested at a sustained rate of over 50,000 records per second, retained for replay by multiple independent consumer applications (a real-time anomaly detector and a batch archiver), and processed in order per device. Which event source is best suited to this ingestion requirement?

choices.text: Amazon SQS FIFO queue, since it guarantees ordering.
Amazon SNS with multiple subscribers for fan-out.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, using the device ID as the partition key.
A single EventBridge custom bus with two rules targeting each consumer.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is designed for high-throughput streaming ingestion with multiple independent consumers reading the same data via enhanced fan-out, and using a per-device partition key preserves ordering within each device's shard. SQS FIFO throughput per message group is far lower and does not naturally support multiple independent replay consumers, and SNS or EventBridge do not provide replay or this level of sustained ordered throughput.

stem: A DevOps team wants to automate response to high-severity Security Hub findings: automatically isolate the affected EC2 instance's security group, but require a human approval step via email before terminating the instance if isolation does not resolve the issue within 30 minutes. Which service is best suited to orchestrate this multi-step, long-running workflow with a wait-for-callback human approval pattern?

choices.text: AWS Step Functions using the waitForTaskToken integration pattern with SNS for the approval notification.
A single Lambda function with a sleep() call for 30 minutes before checking approval status.
AWS Systems Manager Automation with only automatic remediation steps, no human approval capability.
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler configured to invoke a Lambda function every 5 minutes to poll for approval.

explanation: Step Functions natively supports long-running workflows with the waitForTaskToken pattern, allowing a state to pause until an external callback (such as a human approving via an SNS-delivered link) resumes it, with built-in timeout handling. Lambda has a 15-minute maximum execution duration so it cannot sleep for 30 minutes, and polling with EventBridge Scheduler is a far less efficient substitute for native callback support.

stem: A team currently uses an EventBridge rule with an input transformer to reshape events from an SQS queue before invoking a target, but the transformation logic is error-prone, and they want to add an enrichment step that calls an external API to add context before delivery, plus built-in filtering, all without writing a Lambda function purely for plumbing. Which EventBridge feature is purpose-built for this point-to-point flow?

choices.text: EventBridge Pipes, which connects a source directly to a target with built-in filtering, an optional enrichment step, and input transformation.
EventBridge Archive and Replay, which stores events for later reprocessing.
EventBridge Schema Registry, which infers and stores event structure.
A second EventBridge rule chained to the first rule's target.

explanation: EventBridge Pipes is specifically designed for point-to-point integrations between a source like SQS and a target, supporting filtering, an optional enrichment step such as invoking a Lambda function or API, and transformation in a managed way. Archive/Replay and Schema Registry serve different purposes around event storage and schema discovery, and chaining rules adds complexity without a built-in enrichment step.

stem: A company enabled an AWS Organizations CloudTrail trail in the management account and created an EventBridge rule in the management account to detect root user console sign-ins across all accounts, targeting a Lambda function for alerting. During a security drill, a root sign-in occurred in a member account but no alert fired, and the trail is confirmed to be logging correctly across all accounts. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The rule was created on the management account's default event bus, which is where the organization trail's events are delivered, but the rule's event pattern does not correctly match ConsoleLogin events with userIdentity.type of Root.
Organization trails never generate events for member accounts, only for the management account.
EventBridge rules cannot be created in the management account.
Root user activity is never logged by CloudTrail for security reasons.

explanation: An organization trail centralizes logging into the management account and CloudTrail delivers matching events to EventBridge in that same account, so the overall setup is structurally correct; the more likely operational cause is that the event pattern was not scoped correctly to match root sign-ins. Organization trails do capture and forward member account activity, and CloudTrail does log root user actions.

stem: An EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function asynchronously. The team wants to capture the full event payload plus the function's response for successful invocations for downstream analytics, and separately capture failed invocations after retries are exhausted for reprocessing. Which configuration achieves both without writing custom code inside the function to publish results?

choices.text: Configure Lambda destinations with an on-success destination (such as an SQS queue or EventBridge bus) and an on-failure destination (such as a dead-letter SQS queue), rather than relying solely on a DLQ.
Configure only a dead-letter queue, since it captures both successful and failed invocation payloads.
Add try/catch logic inside the Lambda function to manually publish results to SNS on both success and failure.
Enable AWS X-Ray tracing, which automatically stores both successful and failed payloads in S3.

explanation: Lambda destinations natively support routing both successful and failed asynchronous invocation results to different targets and include the invocation payload plus response or error, without extra function code. A DLQ alone only captures failed events after retries are exhausted and does not include response data or successful invocations, and X-Ray provides tracing rather than payload storage.

stem: A central security account has an EventBridge rule intended to receive GuardDuty findings forwarded from ten member accounts via a custom event bus. Findings from nine accounts arrive correctly, but events from the tenth account never appear, even though CloudTrail confirms GuardDuty is generating findings there. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: Whether the tenth account's EventBridge rule target correctly specifies the central account's custom event bus ARN, and whether that event bus's resource policy grants PutEvents permission to the tenth account.
Whether GuardDuty is enabled in the central security account.
Whether the central account's IAM user has AdministratorAccess.
Whether the tenth account has enabled AWS Config.

explanation: Cross-account delivery to a custom event bus requires both a correctly configured rule and target in the sending account pointing at the destination bus ARN, and a resource-based policy on the destination bus authorizing that specific account to call PutEvents; a misconfiguration in either commonly causes silent, single-account delivery failure. GuardDuty status in the central account, IAM user permissions, and Config enablement are all unrelated to whether cross-account events are delivered.

stem: A DevOps engineer needs to programmatically detect when an AWS service is experiencing a regional operational issue that could be affecting the company's specific resources, so an automated workflow can proactively scale out to a backup region. Which AWS Health feature provides account-specific, resource-level event data suitable for this automation, as opposed to general service status information?

choices.text: The AWS Health Dashboard account health view (formerly AWS Personal Health Dashboard), accessible via the AWS Health API, which delivers events scoped to the account's actual resources.
The AWS Health Dashboard service health page, which shows the general operational status of all AWS services for all customers.
The AWS Trusted Advisor service, which checks cost, security, and performance best practices.
AWS Compute Optimizer, which recommends rightsizing based on utilization.

explanation: AWS Health's account-specific view provides events tied to the account's actual affected resources and is accessible via the AWS Health API for automation, unlike the general Service Health Dashboard which reflects broad service-wide status not tied to a specific account's resources. Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer address different concerns, such as best practices and rightsizing, not real-time operational issue notification.

stem: A team needs to run a lightweight remediation Lambda function every 15 minutes to check for and terminate orphaned EC2 instances tagged for cleanup, with no need for multi-step orchestration, retries across multiple services, or workflow state. Which approach introduces the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Create an EventBridge Scheduler schedule that invokes the Lambda function directly every 15 minutes.
Build a Step Functions state machine with a 15-minute wait state in a loop, running continuously.
Create an AWS Config rule with a periodic trigger of 15 minutes that invokes the Lambda function as a remediation action.
Set up a Systems Manager Automation runbook triggered by a CloudWatch Events rule with a rate expression.

explanation: EventBridge Scheduler is purpose-built for simple, recurring invocations like this and is simpler to manage than a long-running Step Functions loop, which incurs unnecessary state transition cost and complexity for a single-step task. AWS Config periodic rules are meant to evaluate resource compliance rather than run arbitrary business logic, and an SSM Automation runbook adds orchestration overhead not needed for a single Lambda invocation.

stem: A compliance team wants to deploy a standardized, versioned collection of about 30 related AWS Config rules and remediation actions covering encryption, logging, and access requirements consistently across 50 accounts in an AWS Organizations structure, with a single compliance score reported per account. What AWS Config feature should they use?

choices.text: AWS Config conformance packs deployed as an organization conformance pack from the management account.
Individual AWS Config rules created manually and repeated in each of the 50 accounts.
AWS Config aggregators configured to write rules into each member account.
AWS Firewall Manager policies applied across the organization.

explanation: Conformance packs bundle Config rules and remediation actions into a single deployable template with an associated compliance score, and organization conformance packs allow deploying that same pack across all or specified accounts from the management account. Aggregators only collect and view compliance data across accounts rather than deploying rules, and Firewall Manager manages network and security services rather than general Config rule compliance.

stem: An Auto Scaling group launches new instances that require several post-boot configuration steps, including installing an agent, registering with a monitoring system, and running a validation script, before they should start receiving traffic. The team wants this orchestrated automatically whenever a new instance launches, with the instance remaining pending until the steps succeed. Which design meets this requirement?

choices.text: Configure an Auto Scaling launch lifecycle hook that transitions the instance to Pending:Wait, with an EventBridge rule matching the lifecycle action event that triggers an SSM Automation runbook to perform the steps and then call CompleteLifecycleAction.
Configure user data in the launch template to run all steps synchronously, with no lifecycle hook needed.
Rely on the default Auto Scaling health check grace period, since it automatically holds instances out of service until configuration completes.
Create a Config rule that evaluates instance configuration after the instance has already entered the InService state.

explanation: A launch lifecycle hook holds the instance in Pending:Wait until CompleteLifecycleAction is called, and pairing it with an EventBridge rule that triggers an SSM Automation runbook allows orchestrated, auditable post-launch configuration before the instance can enter service. User data alone cannot hold the instance out of service pending validation, the health check grace period only affects health check evaluation timing, and a Config rule evaluating an already-InService instance is reactive rather than preventive.

stem: A team is deciding how to remediate AWS Config non-compliance findings for unencrypted EBS volumes. Option one uses AWS Config's built-in automatic remediation feature with an AWS-managed SSM Automation document. Option two uses a custom Lambda function triggered by an EventBridge rule matching Config compliance change events. What is a key operational tradeoff favoring option one for this use case?

choices.text: Config's built-in remediation provides retry logic, execution rate limiting, and a native audit trail tied to the compliance timeline, with less custom code to maintain, at the cost of being limited to what the chosen SSM document supports.
The custom Lambda approach is always cheaper because Config's automatic remediation charges per remediation execution while Lambda has no cost.
Config's built-in remediation cannot use SSM documents and requires Lambda regardless.
The custom Lambda approach provides a built-in compliance audit trail that Config remediation lacks.

explanation: Config's native remediation integrates retry behavior, rate limiting, and audit history directly against the rule's compliance timeline with minimal custom code, though it is constrained by the capabilities of the chosen SSM Automation document, while a custom Lambda approach offers more flexibility but requires building and maintaining that logic and its own audit trail. Lambda invocations are not free, and Config remediation does use SSM documents, so the other options misstate the tradeoff.

stem: An application has a long, resource-intensive instance initialization process, taking 15 or more minutes to warm caches, which makes standard scale-out events too slow to meet demand spikes. The team wants pre-initialized instances ready to be put into service almost immediately when scaling out, without keeping them fully in the live traffic pool and its associated compute cost while idle. Which Auto Scaling feature best fits this need?

choices.text: Auto Scaling warm pools, which keep pre-initialized instances in a stopped or running state outside of the InService pool, ready to be moved in quickly when scaling out.
Launch lifecycle hooks configured with a long Pending:Wait timeout to allow initialization time during every scale-out event.
Scheduled scaling actions that scale out several hours before anticipated demand.
Increasing the health check grace period so instances have more time to become healthy after launch.

explanation: Warm pools maintain a pool of pre-initialized instances, which can be stopped to reduce cost or kept running, separate from the active group, so they can move into service far faster than a cold launch when demand spikes. Lifecycle hooks alone do not pre-initialize instances ahead of time, scheduled scaling does not help with unpredictable spikes, and extending the health check grace period does not reduce actual initialization time.

stem: A central platform team needs a single, queryable view of AWS Config compliance status across 40 accounts and 3 Regions, without logging into each account individually or running cross-account API calls at query time. What should they configure?

choices.text: An AWS Config aggregator in a designated account, using an organization-based aggregator, or authorized individual accounts, to collect configuration and compliance data from all source accounts and Regions.
A single AWS Config rule deployed manually to each of the 120 account-Region combinations.
Cross-account IAM roles that the platform team assumes to run compliance API calls on demand for each account.
An Amazon Athena table queried directly against each account's Config S3 delivery bucket.

explanation: A Config aggregator natively collects configuration and compliance data from multiple source accounts and Regions into one place for unified querying, which is exactly the operational simplification requested. Manually replicating rules does not create a unified view, on-demand role assumption does not provide a persistent aggregated dashboard, and querying individual S3 buckets via Athena requires significant custom setup that duplicates the aggregator's native function.

stem: A Config rule flags non-compliant S3 buckets that lack default encryption, and an automatic remediation action using an SSM Automation document has been attached. Compliance status correctly changes to NON_COMPLIANT, but the remediation action never executes, and the Config console shows no remediation execution history at all. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The IAM role used by the remediation action does not have a trust policy allowing Systems Manager to assume it, or lacks permissions to modify S3 bucket encryption settings.
AWS Config remediation only supports EC2 and IAM resources, not S3 buckets.
The S3 bucket is in a different Region than the Config rule, which is never supported.
Automatic remediation requires manually clicking Remediate in the console every time; there is no fully automatic option.

explanation: If the remediation's assume role lacks the correct trust relationship with Systems Manager or sufficient permissions to perform the action, the automation execution fails to even start, consistent with no execution history appearing at all. Config remediation does support S3 resources via SSM documents, remediation can be configured for fully automatic execution, and this symptom pattern does not match a simple Region mismatch.

stem: A team is building a remediation action that must run for up to 45 minutes to safely drain and replace a fleet of stateful instances, using AWS-provided logic where possible to reduce custom code. Which factor most strongly favors using an SSM Automation runbook over a Lambda function for this specific remediation?

choices.text: SSM Automation runbooks have no execution time limit comparable to Lambda's maximum 15-minute duration, and AWS provides many pre-built automation documents for common infrastructure operations.
Lambda functions cannot be triggered by AWS Config remediation actions at all.
SSM Automation runbooks execute for free while Lambda always incurs cost.
SSM documents can only be written in Python, which the team already uses, while Lambda supports no other option.

explanation: A 45-minute operation exceeds Lambda's hard 15-minute maximum execution duration, whereas SSM Automation runbooks are designed for long-running, multi-step operational tasks, and AWS publishes many pre-built documents for common operations, reducing custom code. Lambda can still be invoked indirectly within remediation flows, SSM Automation is not literally free, and SSM documents support YAML or JSON with various step types rather than being limited to Python.

stem: After deploying a new AMI to an Auto Scaling group's launch template, the operations team expected all running instances to be gradually replaced with the new AMI version, but a week later most instances are still running the old AMI, only being replaced individually as they fail health checks. What should the team do to proactively roll out the new AMI to the entire fleet in a controlled way?

choices.text: Initiate an Auto Scaling instance refresh, which gradually replaces all instances in the group with new ones based on the latest launch template version, respecting a configurable minimum healthy percentage.
Manually terminate every instance in the group at once and let the Auto Scaling group launch replacements.
Update the launch template version again, since updating the launch template automatically triggers replacement of existing instances.
Wait for natural instance replacement due to scaling activities or health check failures, since there is no way to proactively force replacement.

explanation: Updating a launch template only affects instances launched after the update; existing instances are not automatically replaced, which matches the observed symptom. Instance refresh is the purpose-built feature to systematically and safely replace all instances in an Auto Scaling group with new ones based on an updated launch template, using configurable batching and a minimum healthy percentage, unlike a mass manual termination which risks availability.

stem: A Config rule needs to evaluate S3 bucket public access settings immediately whenever a bucket policy changes, rather than waiting for a fixed time interval. Which Config rule trigger type should be configured?

choices.text: The configuration changes trigger type, which evaluates the rule whenever AWS Config records a change to the resource's configuration.
The periodic trigger type, set to the shortest available interval of 1 hour.
Both trigger types must always be enabled together for every Config rule; there is no way to choose only one.
The manual trigger type, run on demand by an administrator.

explanation: A configuration-change trigger causes AWS Config to evaluate the rule as soon as it detects and records a relevant resource configuration change, providing near real-time evaluation rather than waiting on a fixed schedule. A periodic trigger, even at its shortest interval, introduces evaluation lag, and Config rules can be configured with just one trigger type or a combination of both, not a mandatory pairing.

stem: An operations engineer needs a consolidated, cross-account, cross-Region view of patch compliance status for thousands of managed EC2 instances, plus the ability to drill into a specific instance's details such as installed software and file system from a single console interface. Which Systems Manager capability is designed for this?

choices.text: AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager, which provides a unified console view of managed instance inventory, patch compliance, and remote management actions.
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, used to browse instance configuration values.
AWS Systems Manager Change Manager, used to request and approve operational changes.
AWS Systems Manager Documents, which only stores automation scripts.

explanation: Fleet Manager is the Systems Manager console experience purpose-built for viewing and managing a fleet of managed instances, including patch compliance dashboards and remote drill-down actions like file system browsing. Parameter Store manages configuration data rather than instance inventory, Change Manager governs change request workflows, and SSM Documents define automation content rather than provide a fleet visibility dashboard.

stem: A production incident caused thousands of Lambda function errors over a two-hour window across dozens of log streams within one log group. The team needs to quickly identify the top five distinct error messages by frequency without manually scanning each log stream. What is the most efficient approach?

choices.text: Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query using the stats command to group and count occurrences of the error message field across the log group for the two-hour window.
Download all log streams as text files and use a local script to search for the word error.
Create a new CloudWatch alarm and wait for it to report the top error messages.
Manually open each log stream in the console and read through the entries chronologically.

explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights supports a purpose-built query language, including stats by, that can aggregate and count occurrences of a parsed field such as an error message across an entire log group for a specified time range in seconds, directly producing a ranked list. Downloading and manually searching logs is slow and does not scale, alarms only evaluate metrics and thresholds rather than summarizing log content, and manual reading is impractical at this volume.

stem: A CodeDeploy blue/green deployment to an ECS service was configured with CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback, referencing an alarm on the target group's 5XX error count metric. During a recent bad deployment, error rates spiked dramatically, but the deployment completed successfully without rolling back, and the alarm remained in the OK state throughout. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The alarm's evaluation period and datapoints-to-alarm settings were too long relative to the deployment's bake time, so the alarm had not yet transitioned to the ALARM state before CodeDeploy considered the deployment complete.
CodeDeploy does not support CloudWatch alarm-based rollback for ECS deployments, only for EC2 or on-premises deployments.
Automatic rollback based on alarms only works for Lambda deployments, not ECS.
The rollback failed because the deployment used an in-place deployment type rather than blue/green.

explanation: CodeDeploy's alarm-based automatic rollback depends on the referenced CloudWatch alarm actually transitioning to the ALARM state; if the evaluation period and datapoints-to-alarm require sustained breaches over a longer window than the deployment's monitoring or bake time allows, the deployment can finish before the alarm fires. CodeDeploy does support alarm-based rollback for ECS blue/green deployments, and this capability is not restricted to Lambda deployments only.

stem: A CodePipeline execution fails at the build stage, and the pipeline console shows the CodeBuild action failed with a generic build failed status. Where should the engineer look first to find the detailed root cause, such as a specific failing test or compilation error?

choices.text: The CodeBuild project's build logs, viewable either in the CodeBuild console or the associated CloudWatch Logs log group and stream for that specific build run.
The CodePipeline execution history summary page, which contains the full raw build output.
AWS CloudTrail event history, which logs the specific compiler error messages from the build.
The source stage's S3 artifact bucket, which stores a text file of build errors.

explanation: CodeBuild streams detailed build output, including compiler or test failures, to its build logs, accessible through the CodeBuild console or the CloudWatch Logs group configured for the project, making it the authoritative source for build-level diagnostic detail. The CodePipeline console shows only pass or fail status and a summary rather than full output, CloudTrail records API call activity rather than application log content, and the S3 artifact bucket stores build artifacts rather than a formatted error log.

stem: A DevOps team wants every CloudWatch alarm breach on production RDS instances to automatically generate a centralized, trackable operational work item with contextual details such as related resources and runbook links, so engineers can triage and assign it, rather than relying solely on ephemeral SNS email notifications. Which capability should they configure?

choices.text: Configure the CloudWatch alarms to trigger creation of AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter OpsItems, which centralizes operational issues with context, status tracking, and related resource or runbook associations.
Continue using only SNS email notifications, since OpsCenter cannot be integrated with CloudWatch alarms.
Use AWS Config to record the alarm state changes as configuration items.
Create a CloudTrail Insights rule to track the alarm state transitions as a ticketing mechanism.

explanation: Systems Manager OpsCenter aggregates operational issues as OpsItems with status tracking, related resources, and runbook links, and CloudWatch alarms can be configured to automatically create OpsItems when they enter the ALARM state, providing a trackable work item beyond a transient notification. Config records configuration state rather than incident tracking, and CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API activity rather than driving alarm-based ticketing.

stem: A company's public-facing checkout API occasionally fails silently from certain external network paths in ways that internal health checks and server-side metrics do not catch, because the server continues to report healthy while the actual customer-facing request path through CloudFront and external DNS resolution breaks. Which monitoring approach would most directly detect this class of failure before customers report it?

choices.text: Configure a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that periodically executes the actual checkout API call from outside the AWS environment's internal network, following the full external request path, and alarms on failures or latency.
Add more granular CloudWatch custom metrics inside the application server code tracking internal processing time.
Increase the frequency of the ALB target group's internal health checks.
Enable Container Insights on the ECS cluster hosting the checkout service.

explanation: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run configurable scripts on a schedule from AWS-managed locations, exercising the actual external request path including DNS and CDN, which can catch failures that internal, server-side-only monitoring would miss. Internal custom metrics, ALB health checks, and Container Insights all observe from within or close to the application infrastructure and would not detect a break specific to the external network path a customer takes.

stem: An ECS service running on Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer is stuck continuously cycling tasks: new tasks start, briefly register with the target group, then are deregistered and stopped shortly after, and the service never reaches a steady desired count. CloudWatch Logs show the application logging that the server started successfully on its port in each task. What should the engineer check next to diagnose the deregistration?

choices.text: Whether the ALB target group's health check path, port, and success codes are correctly configured to match what the application actually serves, and whether the security group allows the ALB to reach that port.
Whether the ECS task definition's CPU and memory reservations are set to the maximum allowed values.
Whether the ECS cluster has Container Insights enabled.
Whether the Fargate platform version is set to LATEST.

explanation: Since the application logs successful startup, the most likely cause of continuous deregistration is a mismatch between the ALB target group's health check configuration and what the container actually serves, or a security group blocking the ALB's health check traffic to the container port. Task CPU or memory sizing, enabling Container Insights, and the Fargate platform version are unrelated to why a running, logging-healthy application would fail load balancer health checks specifically.

stem: An engineer investigating a production incident finds that several pods in an EKS cluster are in a CrashLoopBackOff state. The engineer wants a consolidated view of container-level CPU and memory metrics correlated with pod restart counts and logs, without manually running commands against each node. Which AWS-native tool provides this consolidated operational view for EKS?

choices.text: Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights, which collects and aggregates cluster, node, pod, and container-level metrics and logs, including restart counts, for EKS into CloudWatch dashboards.
AWS X-Ray, which only provides distributed tracing across HTTP requests, not container resource metrics.
AWS Config, which evaluates the compliance of the EKS cluster's configuration state.
Amazon Inspector, which scans container images for vulnerabilities.

explanation: CloudWatch Container Insights is purpose-built to collect and aggregate metrics such as CPU, memory, and restart counts, along with logs, from EKS clusters, nodes, pods, and containers into a consolidated dashboard, directly supporting this kind of incident triage. X-Ray addresses request-level tracing rather than container resource or restart metrics, Config assesses configuration compliance rather than runtime health, and Inspector performs vulnerability scanning rather than operational monitoring.

stem: A platform team wants a single view that combines distributed trace data with the corresponding CloudWatch metrics and logs for each service in their microservices architecture, so they can pivot from a slow trace directly to the relevant service's dashboard and logs without switching consoles. Which capability provides this integrated experience, building on top of raw X-Ray trace data?

choices.text: CloudWatch ServiceLens, which integrates X-Ray traces with CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms in a unified service map and view.
AWS X-Ray alone, which already displays CloudWatch metrics and logs natively within its trace view without any additional configuration.
AWS Config aggregator, which combines trace and metric data across accounts.
Amazon Detective, which is designed to correlate trace data for security investigations only.

explanation: CloudWatch ServiceLens is the feature that layers X-Ray tracing together with CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms into one integrated service map and console experience, enabling this kind of cross-pivot investigation. Raw X-Ray on its own focuses on trace and segment data without natively surfacing CloudWatch metrics and logs in an integrated view, Config aggregators handle configuration compliance data rather than tracing, and Detective correlates VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and GuardDuty findings for security investigation rather than general application tracing.

stem: Several EC2 instances in a production Auto Scaling group unexpectedly began failing health checks and were replaced by the group. Reviewing AWS Health events for the account reveals a scheduled EC2 instance retirement event listing those exact instance IDs, issued due to underlying hardware degradation. What is the most appropriate root-cause conclusion and follow-up action?

choices.text: The instance failures were caused by underlying hardware degradation flagged by AWS, as documented in the AWS Health event; since Auto Scaling already replaced the instances, the team should verify no application-level impact occurred and consider building automated Health-event-driven proactive replacement to reduce customer-facing impact before AWS-forced retirement.
The AWS Health event is unrelated, since AWS Health only reports informational maintenance windows and cannot report actual instance-impacting hardware issues.
The team should open a support case disputing the retirement, since instance retirements are always avoidable configuration errors on the customer's side.
Because Auto Scaling handled the replacement automatically, no correlation with AWS Health is needed and no further action is warranted.

explanation: AWS Health instance-retirement events specifically flag instances scheduled for retirement due to detected degraded hardware, and correlating this with the observed failures confirms an infrastructure-side root cause rather than an application defect; since Health events are actionable ahead of forced retirement, building automation to react to them proactively reduces the risk of an abrupt, uncontrolled failure. AWS Health does report actionable, resource-specific operational issues rather than only informational items, retirements are not customer configuration errors, and dismissing the event ignores an opportunity for proactive automation.

stem: A production CloudFormation stack has been running stably for months, but the team suspects that an engineer manually modified a security group rule directly in the EC2 console during a recent incident, bypassing the stack. They want to confirm exactly which resources and properties have diverged from the stack's defined template before deciding whether to update the template or revert the manual change. What should they do?

choices.text: Run CloudFormation drift detection on the stack, then review the drift results, which report each resource's drift status and the specific differing properties compared to the expected template-defined configuration.
Delete and recreate the stack, since CloudFormation has no native way to detect out-of-band changes.
Manually compare the template file line-by-line against the current console configuration of every resource in the stack.
Enable AWS Config recording, since CloudFormation does not track resource state beyond initial creation.

explanation: CloudFormation drift detection compares a stack's actual resource configurations against the configuration expected from the template, and reports per-resource drift status along with the specific properties that differ, directly answering what changed and where. Deleting and recreating the stack is unnecessarily destructive, manual line-by-line comparison across many resources is inefficient and error-prone, and while AWS Config could also track changes, it is not required since CloudFormation has this native capability built in.

stem: A company's central security team created an IAM role in a shared services account that third-party auditors assume via STS AssumeRole to review logs. The team wants to prevent the confused deputy problem where the third party's own AWS account could be tricked by an attacker into assuming the role. Which control should be added to the role's trust policy?

choices.text: Require MFA in the trust policy condition using aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent
Add a condition requiring a unique ExternalId value known only to the security team and the third party
Restrict the trust policy to a specific source IP range using aws:SourceIp
Attach a permissions boundary to the role limiting its maximum permissions

explanation: ExternalId is AWS's documented mechanism for the confused deputy problem in cross-account role assumption by third parties, ensuring only requests including the shared secret can assume the role. MFA and source IP conditions address different threats (compromised credentials, network origin) but do not solve confused deputy. Permissions boundaries limit privilege but do not prevent an unauthorized third party from invoking the role.

stem: An account in an OU has an SCP that explicitly denies ec2:TerminateInstances, but a developer in that account still successfully terminates an EC2 instance. The IAM policy simulator shows the developer's identity policy allows the action, and no other SCP in the OU hierarchy grants it. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The SCP was applied to the wrong OU and does not actually affect this account
SCPs only affect the root user, not IAM roles
An explicit Allow in the developer's identity policy overrides the SCP Deny
The account is the organization's management account, which SCPs do not affect

explanation: SCPs never apply to the organization's management account, only to member accounts, so a principal in the management account can still perform the action regardless of SCPs elsewhere. An SCP explicit Deny always overrides an identity-policy Allow in member accounts, so C is false as a general rule, and the scenario evidence doesn't support a misapplied OU or a false claim about root-user-only scope.

stem: An IAM policy denies all actions unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true, intended to force MFA for all API calls. After deployment, automated CI/CD pipelines using an IAM role begin failing all AWS API calls. What is the root cause?

choices.text: IAM roles assumed via AssumeRole cannot support MFA-conditioned policies at all
The aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent key is false or absent for role sessions created without an MFA-authenticated call, so the Deny matches and blocks the automation
CI/CD pipelines must use IAM users instead of roles for MFA to function
The policy needs an explicit Allow statement in addition to the Deny

explanation: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent evaluates to false or is absent when a session was established without MFA at authentication, so a blanket Deny-unless-MFA policy also blocks non-interactive automation roles that cannot supply MFA. The fix is typically to scope the MFA requirement away from automation roles, not to abandon roles for users, and roles can carry MFA context; it simply is not present for machine-to-machine calls.
